headline: Screen: 'Utamaro,' Painter of Women':Japanese Film at the Carnegie Hall Cinema Title Role Is Portrayed by Kazuo Hasegawa
abstract: IF it was a painting of a Japanese landscape you might have wanted in the 18th century, you would have gone—were you a Japanese noble-man—to an artist on the order of Prof. Eisen Kanoh, who painted in the traditional bees-and-blossoms style.But if it was a painting of a woman you were after, a slit-eyed geisha or a giggling prostitute, you would have gone to Utamaro, a man of the people who painted in what I am told might be described as the 18th-century counterpart of the contemporary George Petty cover-girl style.Utamaro is the enterprising fellow who is floridly featured in the flimsy, foolish, sentimental but prettily photographed Japanese color film "Utamaro, Painter of Women," which came to the Carnegie Hall Cinema yesterday.Don't look for anything other than some handsome décor in this film, which seems to have as its chief recommendation the fact that it was produced by the same man who produced the classic Japanese film "Gate of Hell." It is simply a stiff kimono drama about an artist whose lively pictures of lusty girls become so popular through reproduction in the woodblock process that it rouses the jealousy of a traditional painter. Professor Eisen, who has his cut-throats break our poster painter's arm.In this disabled condition, the hero is cruelly neglected by all the dazzling prostitutes and geishas who previously threw themselves at his feet—literally, in the Japanese fashion—in order to get him to glamorize them with his brush. (One of them he has uniquely distinguished by painting a huge design for a tattoo on her back and hip—a piece of artcraft which you can imagine is more interesting than painting a picture on a wall.)But at least he is not neglected by a beautiful maiden who lives next door and has worshiped him with pure devotion. She bilks a wealthy young man of the upper class to rush back to the side of the stricken artist and help him regain the use of his crippled arm.The story, as you can see, is flapdoodle, and it is clumsily written and staged by Keigo Kimura, who has yet to master the equivalent of a Hollywood silent-film style. It is likewise stiffly played by Kazuo Hasegawa, who was the importunate lover in "Gate of Hell," and a bevy of beautiful Japanese actresses who pass so rapidly they are hard to tell apartIt is pretty to look at however—nicely set up, costumed and photographed in the bright and pastel colors that are so subtly blended in Japanese films. And once in a while it gives a coy glimpse of a discreetly disrobed female form, thus maintaining the romantic notion of what it's like in an artist's studio.Adequate English subtitles translate the Japanese dialogue.

headline: Screen: 'Male Companion' Begins Run:Farce Finds Director Beginning to Tire
abstract: EVIDENTLY Philippe de Broca considers the lilies of the field more worthy of emulation than the ants or the beavers, let us say. In three previous lightweight French farces—"The Five Day Lover," "The Joker" and "The Love Game"—he has fervently recommended heroes who have toiled not, neither have they spun, yet they have flourished with the casualness of lilies. These heroes have all been played by Jean-Pierre Cassel.Now, in his latest, "Male Companion" ("Un Monsieur de Compagnie"), which opened at the Baronet yesterday, Mr. de Broca is celebrating a fellow who frankly shirks work with a fierce élan. Trained by an elegant uncle to perceive that the way to succeed is spend one's time idling and playing, this fellow just takes things as they come. The things are mostly chic, compliant females. And the fellow is again Mr. Cassel.Mr. de Broca has a wry thought and a fair enough formula for a film, but to spin it into winning entertainment a certain amount of work must be done, first by the scriptwriters and then the director, both of which Mr. de Broca is. And along toward the middle of the picture it looks as though he has adopted the hero's philosophy as his own.It starts out well enough with the loafer lodging himself cozily in the pad of a charitable friend's Montmartre mistress, whom Irina Demick appropriately enacts. Then he finds a nice home as the playmate of an eccentric aristocrat who is nuts about trains. There he helps operate the model system and sleeps in a room that is built like a compartment in a wagon-lits. And here, we might note, the picture reaches its comic peak.For Mr. de Broca has managed to develop this antic conceit into a whirligig of nonsense that has the frenzy of old-time slapstick farce. The aspect of two grown-up fellows, Mr. Cassel and Jean-Claude Brialy, rigged out in trainmen's uniforms and playing with small electric trains is a sight in itself. And the clatter of whistles, wheels and bells coming over the hi-fi, and the rocking of the compartment at night, or the pouring of smoke through the window when Mr. Cassel opens it, makes for some funny business. The two actors are up to it.But the hero and Mr. de Broca both seem to find this phase too much, and the picture falls into aimless nonsense when the exhausted loafer flees to Italy. Here he fumbles through various adventures—with a pizza-maker's wife, played by voluptuous Sandra Milo; with an attorney (Adolfo Celi), who is bereaved by the loss of a son but has five daughters to comfort him—and his guest; with a Greek connoisseur of paintings (Dalio), who also likes pretty and marriageable dames; with a charming secretary, played by Catherine Deneuve.There are random laughs in this last part. Mr. de Broca pulls a swiftie now and then, and Mr. Cassel is continually his breezy, beaming self. The scenery in Rome is delightful and the color is excellent. But the fun is progressively less lively. It apparently took too much work.Also on the bill is an engaging 20-minute documentary film, shot in Eastern Nigeria. It is entitled "The Ancestors" and it describes the ceremonial rituals the Nigerian bush natives perform, and the wood carvings they create in connection with the deaths of their foremost men. It tells a fascinating story of a tradition that is sure to pass. Anthropologists should love it. It is in color and was made by André Libik.

headline: Outrages
abstract: TWO documentary films of such unfortunately painful contrast that their showing together was a tasteless offense were shown as the early program in Philharmonic Hall last night.The first was the Canadian National Film Board's "Memorandum," which is a mature and profoundly sensitive account of a reunion of Jewish survivors at Auschwitz, at Belsen and at other Nazi death camps on the occasion of the 20th anniversary of their liberation. The second was Jean Rouch's "The Lion Hunters," a grisly and tedious report of a visit with a tribe of primitive people in the backlands of Nigeria."Memorandum" so frankly and feelingly reminds us of the horrible things that occurred in the death camps, and then intercuts so shrewdly and with such philosophical intent a general contemplation of the German people as they are today that it accomplishes magnificently its purpose of making us comprehend both the deathless outrage of those who suffered and the uselessness of continuing to hate.In an hour of superior documentation, accompanied by the most tasteful music and narration, it sums up the present desirable posture that one should have toward an eternal historical shame.To see, after this splendid picture, Mr. Rouch's unskillful travelogue, which tops off a lengthy and redundant account of how the natives prepare for the hunt with some garish and hideous color pictures of assorted animals being trapped and killed with poisoned arrows, was to have one's intelligence and sensibilities pointlessly abused and disturbed. Are the directors of the festival so cynical that they see any possible social or ethnical connection between these two films?

headline: Bulgarian Film Traces Conflict With the State
abstract: "DETOUR," the two-character Bulgarian film that opened yesterday at the Fifth Avenue Cinema, is a gentle, brief encounter on the outskirts of Sofia. The movie, directed by Grisha Ostrovski and Todor Stoyanov, won the first prize at the 1967 Moscow Film Festival, a fact that—if it does nothing else—should certify the movie's earnest, somewhat déjà vu respectability.Ivan Andonov, a handsome, middle-aged engineer, and Nevena Kokanova, a pretty archeologist, were lovers during their university days—in the late 1940's when young Bulgarians danced to "Amapola" and "The Dipsy Doodle" and postponed their own pleasures to serve the socialist experiment. Seven-teen years later they meet by chance, after each has married someone else and pursued a successful career. In short, chronologically structured flashbacks, they recall their affair, talk briefly of renewing it, and then part.The film moves easily between the two time periods, is nicely acted, particularly by Miss Kokanova, who suggests the young Sylvia Sidney, and is told with a good deal of understated feeling and humor. I imagine that the manner in which it plays with time and acknowledges the conflict between the individual and the state might seem quite unconventional in Moscow.In New York where, on almost any day of the week, one has access to some of the best movies made over the last 60 years, "Detour" can be of special interest only as an example of what the late-starting Bulgarian movie industry can do. The film is technically good, artistically eclectic, and as cinematically zippy as a warm Orange Crush.The Bulgarian dialogue is translated by English subtitles that are strung out to practically the full width of the wide-screen image. Reading them is like watching a tennis match.

headline: Impact of New Directors Series:Works of 5 Countries Shown at Museum Self-Discovery Theme Found in Each Piece
abstract: The second five programs in the New Directors/New Films series just completed at the Museum of Modern Art offered movies from Switzerland, Hungary, Cuba, England and the United States. They are all first or second features by youngish directors generally unknown here, and, taken all together, they constitute the loveliest body of new cinema work that I have seen in some years. Taken individually, there are distinctions to be made, and I have my favorites—the Swiss "Salamander" and the Cuban "Memories of Underdevelopment," both already acquired for United States distribution—and my least favorite also—the Hungarian "Horizon."Pal Gabor's "Horizon" is a sensitive, slightly too artful study of a Budapest teenager who skips his school examination, quits his job, and takes off in a few directions that his mother, whom he loves, and the girl who loves him can't follow. He ends up with a factory job as dumb as the office job he's just left, but along the way he had had a few adventures and made some starts in the very crucial process of self-discovery.To a considerable degree, self-discovery is what "Horizon" is about. It is also what all the other four films are about, and it constitutes a theme, for at least this part of the series, of quite astonishing consistency.This search for a sense of oneself is not simply a preoccupation of the young. The hero of Tomas Guterrez Alea's "Memories of Underdevelopment" is 38 years old, and he is the most boyishly lost of the lot. But the search is a highly individualized activity (consider even the title of Barney Platts-Mills's "Private Road," in which the identity crisis grows out of a love affair that fails between two attractive upper-middle class English kids) and one that presupposes the value, the ultimate legitimacy of personal perceptions.Sometimes such priority of values seems hard won, as in David Schikele's fine "Bushman." Mr. Schikele's film, an unusual blend of documentary and fictional vignettes, deals with a Nigerian (Paul Eyam Nzie Okpokam) teaching at San Francisco State, who in fact, and in the middle of production, was deported by the Government for the alleged possession of a bomb. The movie ends with the deportation, but despite all provocation its mood is relaxed, tolerantly ironic, sophisticated—with a delight in subtle complexities that seems, in its lack of stridency, post-revolutionary.Even more complex, and distinctly more post-revolutionary, Mr. Alea's "Memories of Underdevelopment" begins as its bourgeois hero contentedly sends his wife into Stateside exile and settles back in his Havana apartment to wait for whatever will come next. A lot comes, much of it very funny, and none of it the triumph of ideology you might have expected. Mr. Alea's model is early-to-middle Antonioni, but he is dealing with real rather than mythic history, and unlike Antonioni, all his perceptions are touched by wit.Alain Tanner's "Salamander" acknowledges its debts more directly, as its heroes, a pair of writers named Pierre and Paul (of course, after Truffaut's "Jules and Jim") develop a story based on the life of a shop girl named Rosemond, who may or may not have shot her uncle in the shoulder. They meet Rosemond (Bulle Ogier), are both seduced by her, and ultimately drop the story, find themselves, and lose the girl into a kind of mild insanity—which is her freedom in this rich, tough, technically modest and marvelously alert new film.

headline: And Nowa Finnish Film Festival ':Change Is Sought Old-Fashioned Personality
abstract: Just try telling someone that you're off to a festival of Finnish films and the response is likely to be, "Did you say finished films?"Although film has become an international art, it's still hard to imagine that such countries as Brazil, Nigeria and, yes, Finland, have small film industries of their own. To let filmgoers here know that Finland is not just the country of saunas and Sibelius, the library at Lincoln Center and Cinema Dimensions, a distribution company, are presenting, through Saturday, 13 Finnish films in the library's museum.In recent years, the only Finnish director to emerge with any recognition was Jorn Donner, and most of his films have been Swedish productions. His bubbly sex comedy, "To Love," starring Harriet Andersson, was shown several years ago at the New York Film Festival and then had a modest run here. Donner's worldly film, influenced by Ingmar Bergman's light comedies, had a kicky champagne spirit.Change Is SoughtI remember "To Love" because it aroused my curiosity about Finland—and the Finnish movie industry. Donner is not included in the festival. The sponsors understandably wanted to introduce other directors. His presence was missed."There's a lot of talent in Finland," says Richard Anobile of Cinema Dimensions, "but the films are not considered commercial on foreign markets." He's right, but he hopes to change the situation with Finnish-American co-productions.The grand old man of Finnish theater and films is apparently Edvin Laine, whose three-hour epic of Finnish history, "Under the Northern Star," opened the festival and will be shown again this week. The color, widescreen film, based on a popular Finnish trilogy, might be described as Finland's "Gone With the Wind."With a big cast in interweaving stories covering two generations, "Star" shows the plucky nation's suffering and stumbling progress—from a grand duchy of Russia to independence and civil war. Like a Cecil B. DeMille pageant, the canvas is almost too cumbersome, the characters are cardboard and yet, despite elements of operatic kitsch, the director knows how to build suspense and pathos while giving a thumbnail sketch of Finnish history.Old-Fashioned PersonalityHis plot devices are old-fashioned, but you have to admire the unabashed sentiment of his last shot: a bedraggled soldier returning home in the howling rain. Obviously there was a personality behind this work, which I did not feel at all in the two other "modern" movies I saw."Worker's Diary" by Risto Jarva deals with contemporary life in Finland, which rises like a glassy skyscraper on the edge of a primeval forest. It touches, but only blandly, the monotony—and isolation—in the marriage of a clerical secretary and her husband, a factory foreman. It's almost as if the director were embarrassed by the bleakness of his material."Green Widow," by Jaakko Pakkasvirta, is a suburban housewife who finds relief from her philandering, boorish husband with a mini-affair of her own. The mad housewife, ably played by Eija Pokkinen, is the sort of striking Finn who usually runs to Paris—one of the exotic Left Bank Lapps.But this "Green Widow" is strangely repressed. The social mores reflected in her life are related to yesterday, to the late nineteen-fifties. I refuse to believe that the ultimate Finnish decadence is a marijuana cigarette smoked in the late afternoon.My impression from these films is that the Finns have resources. What they really need is boldness—and cinematic vision.

headline: What's Doing in LAGOS
abstract: THE FACE OF THE CITY—In Lagos there is a degree of integration between residents and foreigners rarely found in other African capitals. There are unintegrated slums, of course, beginning at the foot of Carter Bridge on the island of Lagos, but many Nigerians live in the sprawling middle‐class housing de velopments of Apapa, Surulere and Ikeja and also in the plushly suburban mansions of Ikoyi Island, where most foreign diplomats and businessmen reside. Nigeria is under military rule, and by law politicking is not permitted, but ebullient Lagos residents talk long and loud about the proposed return to civilian rule in 1976.Three schools of thought on the subject are most often heard: 1. That the military should continue to rule. 2. That a civilian government should take over. 3. That the new government should consist of a combination of civilian and military leaders. Other current topics  of conversation—in English, the official language of this former British possession, and in various African languages—include traffic jams, housing shortages, the building boom and other indicators of a fast‐paced, oil‐bolstered economic boom. In addition, people are talking about what promises to be the biggest of all African cultural celebrations, the Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture, which is scheduled for November and December, 1975. Early indications are that as many as 100,000 visitors will come to this city of about a million people for the festival. “Where are we going to put them?” residents ask. Officials are replying by building a new city for at least 50,000 guests on the outskirts of town. After the festival, the development is to become apartments for local families.

headline: Book Ends
abstract: Future Ford. In an analogously enviable position to Coward, McCann & Geoghegan, who found themselves with a biography of Gerald Ford on their hands when Mr. Nixon resigned, is a small publisher called The Third Press. The company commissioned a biography of Vice President Ford (as he then was) around the first of this year, and the writer they chose to do it was the then Washington bureau chief of The Detroit News, Jerald F. terHorst. So Third Press now has on their hands the nearly completed MS. of “Gerald Ford and the Future of the Presidency,” which they will rush through for late October publication. Joseph Okpaku, the Nigerian‐born president of The Third Press, explained his prescience matter‐of‐factly. He was looking around for a political book related to the Watergate troubles (as who wasn't?) and after several possibilities fell through, decided to focus on the post‐Watergate situation. This led him to zero in on Mr. Ford as “the future Mr. Republican”; the remaining problem was to choose an author. Mr. terHorst had the obvious credentials of being from Mr. Ford's home state and a respected political journalist; he also fit Mr. Okpaku's criterion of avoiding an “Eastern liberal” writer. Events moved apace and as the deadline for an ad announcing the book drew near, the title was not set, though “Gerald Ford: Past, Present and Future” was a front runner. But as Mr. Nixon's departure became more urgently likely the present title was chosen, the day before the resignation. Mr. terHorst's appointment as press secretary did not alter the content of the book in any way, Mr, Okpaku said. The President merely told him to “be objective—nobody's perfect.” So the promise, at least, is of an “open biography.” The book ‘ends with Mr. Ford's accession and Mr. terHorst's speculations on what stamp Mr. Ford will place on the office.’ The Third Press is sometimes vaguely thought of as a black publishing house, but actually Mr. Okpaku has always sought a general list. At any rate, he is anticipating the company's first best seller, plans a 50,000‐copy first printing and expects to double that. Incidentally, Mr. Okpaku does not always guess right politically. Before the French Presidential elections, he commissioned a book by Francois Mitterand, the Socialist candidate, who lost.

headline: Which Tribe Do You Belong to?
abstract: Travel‐writing is one of the less harmful expressions of perverse restlessness, an interlude for the portable imagination; all it takes is a strong stomach, a sense of occasion and an appetite for landscapes of dazzling sameness. There are mishaps, of course: a Lagos crowd looks as if it's going to trample you to death, a bantering African tries to snatch your expensive wristwatch, $1,000 gets' nicked from your hotel bedroom, and Pier Paolo Pasolini won't stop taking pictures of the colorful natives. But it is fairly glamorous as all travel seems in retrospect. (“Why, are those really the famous Mountains of the Moon?”) Before putting on my pith helmet and sitting down to read Alberto Moravia's collection of articles from 10 years' junketing in Africa, I read the South African novelist, Nadine Gordimer's superb new book “The Conservationist” and found myself writing later, “There are so many versions of Africa it is almost possible to believe that the fixed place doesn't exist; not a continent, but an occasion.” Miss Gordimer writes as a resident, and her version is a credible nightmare; Signor Moravia writes as a visitor, and his is much sunnier. Here he is describing an African dance: “... it must be said that the dance is merely the most striking aspect of the contagious primitive rhythm which the African has introduced into the modern world. This rhythm, which now seems to us an indivisible, ingrained part of industrial civilization, comes, on the contrary, straight from prehistoric, archaic times. It is the most precious gift that the African has ...”

headline: Screen:' Abby,' About a Black Family and Exorcism
abstract: If "The Exorcist" luridly indicated that a white girl plagued by demons could be a problem, "Abby," which landed unsteadily at the Penthouse and RKO 86th Street theaters yesterday, illustrates that a black girl, if not an amused moviegoer, can also be unsettled by dire manufactured powers. As "the story of a woman possessed" who is finally cleansed of those devils, "Abby" is more silly than shocking even if it seems to take itself seriously.Blame all the ersatz deviltry on William Marshall, as the film's imposingly learned minister-archeologist who unwittingly looses evil forces by digging up an ancient religious artifact in Nigeria that invades the body of his young, lovely, decent daughter-in-law back home in Louisville, Ky. And, of course, Carol Speed, as Abby, his daughter-in-law, begins to behave more and more like a rampaging hooker than a loving bride, churchwoman and dedicated community worker.Her personal poltergeist—which sets off a series of mysterious sounds and furies, including slamming doors and flying furniture, as well as sexual and physical assaults—threatens to send the family, a hospital staff and the cops off the deep end. But not before Mr. Marshall, wearing exotic garb and intoning an exotic religious ritual, steps in climactically to exorcise and save the plagued Abby from her destructive alter ego.Mr. Marshall does manage to be dignified despite the mumbo-jumbo he's involved with. But Miss Speed, whose lips turn purple and whose voice turns basso profundo in spewing obscenities in her "possessed" state, is energetic, if unconvincing, as the afflicted Abby, Terry Carter and Austin Stoker are believably confused and frightened as her minister husband and cop brother, respectively.As her distraught mother, Juanita Moore delivers one of the film's most intelligent lines. She comforts her ailing daughter at one point with, "I'm gonna get you a cold towel for your head. It'll make you feel better." A cold towel could help a viewer, too.

headline: Film: African Adventure:'Countdown at Kusini' About Political Plot
abstract: "Countdown at Kusini" is the sort of movie that illustrates what happens when achievement falls short of aims.Conceived as a conventional melodramatic vehicle for the transmission of excitement and as a medium for explanation of the black revolution in Africa to an alien audience, this movie—filmed in and around Lagos, Nigeria—emerges as subpar adventure and less than lucid ideology.For the most part, it concerns itself with a plot by multinational corporations—the postcolonial villains—to remove a black revolutionary leader through the efforts of a French mercenary and his black and white collaborators. A woman dedicated to the revolution and an American jazz musician, drawn more to the woman than to politics, provide the romantic interest and the effort to thwart the mercenary.The script is burdened with lamentable lines that require the best efforts of Ossie Davis, Ruby Dee and Greg Morris in the lead roles to overcome and failing that, invite the use of nearly constant music to drown out the dialogue.Compounding the troubles are the occasional mismatched shots and, in effect, an epilogue that vitiates its educational strivings.

Chuco, the younger one, has no identity except (or that of his gang, which leads him first to paint-sniffing and then to disaster."Boulevard Nights," which opens today at the Cinerama and other theaters, trivializes the Mexican-American experience by equating it with the melodrama of many other minor movies about gang wars. The film, written by Desmond Nakano and directed by Michael Pressman, is so busy trying to meet the needs of a conventional narrative that it appears to have no point of view about its characters. When we watch them suffer and die in foolish pursuits, the movie is merely sightseeing.With the possible exception of Mr. De La Paz, whose haunted looks suggest someone deeply troubled, the actors are not very good. Mr. Pressman begins one key scene by pointing the camera at the sky and then panning down to the action on the ground. When a director starts a scene by taking pictures of the sky, it usually means he's not got very much on his mind.

headline: GOING OUT Guide; WIN, PLACE AND SHOW OLD IRONSIDES LADY IN WAITING
Film: 'Black Goddess':Search for Ancestors
abstract: "BLACK GODDESS" is really two films, one of them an historical melodrama in the manner of "Roots" and the other a fiery, forceful tribute to contemporary African culture. "Black Goddess," a Brazilian/Nigerian co-production in the Museum of Modern Art's New Films/New Directors program, was written and directed by Ola Balogun in something approaching a documentary style, although it tells a fictitious story. It will be shown at the museum this evening at 8:30 and tomorrow at 6 P.M.The story ostensibly concerns a young Nigerian, Batatunde, who is sent by his dying father to Brazil, where one of his ancestors was carried off in slavery centuries earlier. Batutunde's mission in Brazil is to find out what became of his family, and by the end of the film this is revealed, in flashback sequences that are affecting but relatively conventional by comparision with the rest of the material. The modern-day sequences, far more fascinating, follow Batatunde into Rio de Janeiro and Bahia, as he seeks out an African community and observes dances and religious customs. There is a pretty young woman who functions as a kind of medium at one religious meeting, and soon enough Batatunde has fallen in love. Mr. Balogun scarcely misses such opportunities to keep the material as entertaining as it is instructive.A commanding young actress, Sonia Santos, plays both this young woman and one of Batatunde's forebears, a slave who is pursued and raped by her white owner as she falls in love with Batatunde's captured relative. Mr. Balogun lets this part of the film grow slightly feverish and familiar, but it remains dramatically effective even then.

headline: U.N. REPORT ON PRESS IS CAUSING CONCERN
abstract: The United Nations has quietly moved toward endorsing a report that some Western journalists fear would strengthen government control of the press.   In a little noticed action last month, the General Assembly voted without dissent that nations should ''take into account'' in framing communications policy the recommendations of a commission headed by Sean MacBride of Ireland. Among other things, the commission proposes what the press should and should not cover, criticizes private newsgathering organizations and urges more public ownership of the press.   The document, ''Many Voices, One World,'' was prepared for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. Its New York director, Doudou Diene of Nigeria, said the Assembly's action ''gives a strong political support to the main reccomendations of the MacBride report.''

headline: RICE SHORTAGE IN NIGERIA BRINGS CHARGES OF CORRUPTION
abstract: Despite the spectacular growth in Nigeria's oil income in recent years, the nation has been unable to keep up with the demand for rice, the price of which has tripled in the last six months.   The shortage has led to charges that officials under President Shehu Shagari, who was elected in 1979 on an anticorruption platform, have benefited from the price increases by manipulating supplies through the use of import licenses.   For millions of urban Nigerians, the biggest purchase of each month is the 110-pound bag of rice that feeds the family. Before Christmas a bag that could be imported for $40 was selling here for $150. A well-paid office worker earns $450 a month, and a laborer gets a minimum wage of $150.

headline: GUERILLA CHIEF DISCUSSES GUNS, GOALS, WHITES
abstract: THE Carter Administration ran out of time last week in its fouryear effort, with Western European countries, to end the guerrilla war in South-West Africa. Declaring in Geneva that it would be ''premature'' to arrange a cease-fire now, Danie Hough, South Africa's administrator-general for the territory also called Namibia, brought negotiations under United Nations auspices to a standstill.   The insurgent South-West Africa People's Organization, commonly known as SWAPO, said it would ask the Security Council to impose mandatory sanctions against South Africa. That could pose a difficult choice for the Reagan Administration, which is reportedly inclined to give priority to economic and strategic interests in South Africa. Other African countries, notably Nigeria, an important oil exporter, strongly support independence for Namibia.   To clarify SWAPO's intentions, Joseph Lelyveld, The New York Times correspondent in southern Africa, interviewed Sam Nujoma, the insurgents' leader. Excerpts follow from their conversation during the conference in Mr. Nujoma's hotel suite in Geneva.

headline: GOING OUT GUIDE
abstract: HISTORICAL ART   The West African kingdom of Benin, in what is now Nigeria, has existed for 700 years. European ambassadors were sent there 400 years ago. It thrived in the 17th and 18th centuries; conquering much of the surrounding area and trading in palm oil, ivory, pepper and slaves. Life there was traditionally complex, sophisticated and rigidly hierarchical. And this was reflected in what Benin is now principally known for - its art: wood and ivory carvings and metal work, some of which dates back to the 13th century.   Much Benin art found its way into foreign hands. Benin City, the kingdom's metropolis and now capital of Benin province, was burned by British troops in 1897 during what was called the Punitive Expedition. The British acted after some Beninites killed members of a British delegation that had been told not to visit the city but did so anyway. The British troops ransacked the area and took back to England some 2,500 bronzes.

headline: LINKAGE IN AFRICA
abstract: What hints there have been of the Reagan Administration's likely outlook toward black Africa suggest, not surprisingly, an emphasis on stability. Some American conservatives have talked about trying to destabilize the Government party, the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola, known by its initials M.P.L.A., which won power in 1975 with Soviet and Cuban help and still has perhaps 17,000 Cuban soldiers in the country. headline: ART: THE GLORIES OF BENIN'S ROYALTY
abstract: ''IMAGES OF POWER: The Royal Court of Benin'' at the Grey Art Gallery and Study Center (33 Washington Place) comprises 65 works, most of which date from the 16th to the 18th centuries. Drawn mainly from private collections in New York, these bronze heads and plaques, together with miscellaneous works in ivory, wood and terra cotta, celebrate the lives of the Oba, or god-kings of the city-state of Benin. Obichere, professor of history at the University of California at Los Angeles and Ilorin University in Nigeria, and William Fagg of the British Museum. headline: ISOLATION SAPS AMERICANS ON THE OIL RIGS OF NIGERIA
abstract: They come here with the rich black soil of the Mississippi delta, the gumbo of Louisiana or the dust of Texas still on their boots, and 28 days later they fly back to whatever patch of America they call home, and 28 days after that they are back in this oilfield for another tour. Such is the bubble in which they live that not one of them can name the President of Nigeria.   Their employer here off the mouth of the Escravos River, the Gulf Oil Company of Nigeria, though elsewhere along the coast it could be Shell or Mobil, has charted the effect of the 28-day shift on these American oil workers. The chart reveals that most accidents occur and productivity declines on the first three and the last two days of a man's tour. ''We look for all our problems then,'' said Jim Lake, a Texan and a drilling superintendent.

headline: PIRATES OF LAGOS: ONCE AN ANNOYANCE, NOW A MAJOR THREAT
abstract: Piracy in the harbor here, for years a petty annoyance, has reached such an outrageous level that shipping agents representing lines from the United States, Europe and the Far East are concerned that their maritime unions might boycott the port.   One ship was recently attacked 12 times in a five-day period. The port, one of the busiest in Africa, never has fewer than 50 ships at anchor at one time, and it is estimated that every freighter that has called here regularly in the last few years has been attacked at least once.   The European Economic Community has formally protested the lawlessness to the Nigerian Foreign Ministry. The Netherlands recently protested twice in two weeks. And when a committee of the shipping trade group of the Nigerian Chamber of Commerce and Industry asked the police to begin an antipirate patrol, it was told by the inspector general of police that the police did not have the means to do it.

headline: BRITAIN TURNS ON THE POMP FOR NIGERIAN PRESIDENT
abstract: President Shehu Shagari of Nigeria came to Britain this week, in a glittering state visit full of symbols of his nation's expanding role in the world.   In a week that both sides were eager to portray as an important watershed in the relationship between their nations, Mr. Shagari was treated by businessmen, by the Government, by the royal family and by private citizens as the much-respected leader of a country that is not only very large and very rich but also - just lately - democratic.  Mr. Shagari, who came to office in October 1979 after 13 years of military rule in Nigeria, is one of the third world's few democratically elected heads of state. headline: U.S. PLANS A MISSION TO SOUTHERN AFRICA
abstract: The Reagan Administration has ended a major policy review and plans to announce that it will send a high-level mission to Africa to explore ways of bringing about the independence of South-West Africa, as well as settling other key problems with South Africa.   Administration officials said today that the White House was expected to announce shortly, perhaps as soon as Monday, that Chester A. Crocker, the Assistant Secretary of State-designate for African Affairs, would visit the so-called front-line states of Angola, Botswana, Mozambique, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe, as well as South Africa.   A purpose of the mission, officials said, is to open a constructive dialogue with South Africa on ways to bring about change in that country, while reassuring the black African leaders of the Administration's interest in finding an internationally acceptable formula for ending South Africa's control of South-West Africa, also known as Namibia. headline: ARCO FORGOES COSTLY AFRICAN OIL
abstract: The Atlantic Richfield Company is giving up its right to 60,000 barrels a day of expensive, high-quality Nigerian crude oil, a move that oil industry sources say is illustrative of the current oil glut. headline: WEST AFRICA'S CREEPING DEMOCRACY
abstract: The Nigerian capital of Lagos, last stop on a recent six-nation tour of West Africa, is the richest, dirtiest, most disorderly city of the region.   Swollen to a population of about 2.5 million, it is the archetypal boom and shanty town. The atmosphere is a combination of the ravaged South Bronx, complete with gangs of armed marauders, and the Klondike, complete with cherry-size gold nuggets on a man's elaborately embroidered tunic.   When electricity and water supplies break down, as they often do, when two or three planeloads of passengers with confirmed tickets scramble and shove to get on one overbooked plane, when officials just don't show up for appointments, people shrug and say, ''This is Africa.''

headline: ANTI-APARTHEID UNIT PUBLISHES SPORTS LIST
abstract: More than 250 athletes and officials from 22 countries, among them 63 Americans, were included yesterday in the first United Nations Centre Against Apartheid blacklist for havig participated in sports exchanges in South Africa during the last year.  Named on the list were such prominent professionals as Gary Player, the South African golfer; Guillermo Vilas, the Argentine tennis player; Lester Piggott, the British jockey, andCarlos Reutemann, the Argentine car driver.   Americans in eight sports were listed.  They included Lee Trevino and 10 other golfers; Stan Smith, Bob Lutz, Dick Stockton, Pat Dupre and 24 other tennis players; six boxers, along withe athletes from track and field, equestrian events, life saving, motor racing and water skiing.  The release of the list coincided with meetings yesterday in Washington between President Reagan and Rolloef F.  Botha, South Africa's foreign minister.  "In publishing the rirst issue of the 'Register of Sports Contacts with South Africa,' the document said, "the Special Committee reiterates the importance of the cessation of all exchanges with apartheid sport as a contribution to the international efforts for the elimination of apartheid and in support of freedom in South Africa.  It hopes that the register will facilitate appropriate action by governments, organizations and individuals in the capaign for the boycott of apartheid sport." B. Akporode Clark, the Nigerian ambassador to the United Nations, described the publication of the blacklist as "one of the most important developments in the current activity against apartheid." Mr. Clark said athletes who appeared on the list, would be unwelcome in African countries and that the Supreme Council on Sport in Africa had urged other countries to deny entry to the athletes for competitions.

headline: KUWAIT'S NEW ROLE IN HAWAII
abstract: After the Arab oil embargo in 1973-74, James F. Gary, chairman of Pacific Resources Inc., began traveling the world looking for reliable sources of crude oil for his oil refinery. headline: Notes; AFRICAN TOURS THAT EMPHASIZE CULTURE
abstract: Four travel and study programs in Africa that emphasize meeting writers and artists and visiting institutions of learning as well as traditional sightseeing are being offered this summer by the American Forum for International Study, an organization founded in 1968 to encourage cultural exploration of Africa.   ''Introduction to Africa,'' a one-week tour to Senegal and Gambia costs $1,280 a person in double occupancy. On the tour's itinerary in Senegal are Goree Island, a fortress at which slaves were held for shipment; Dakar, the Senegalese capital; Thies, site of a tapestry factory; Cayer, a fishing village; Joal Fadiouth, a community on three islands and Keur Mousse, a Roman Catholic monastery. Banjul, the Gambian capital, and Gufere, the village made famous by Alex Haley's ''Roots'' are also part of the week's program.   Another tour, which is called ''Cross African Societies,'' takes its members to Nigeria, Kenya, Ethiopia and Egypt as well as to Senegal. Among that tour's highpoints are the Nigerian city Ibadan, a center of the Yoruba people; the game parks of Kenya; Addis Ababa; Cairo; Luxor; Aswan and Abu Simbel. The itinerary includes two schools of special interest in Kenya, the school for the blind at Thika and the college-preparatory Alliance High School, outside of Nairobi. The three-week tour costs $2,980 a person.

headline: ART: MET PRESENTS AFRICAN ANTHOLOGY
abstract: FOR the second time in less than a year, the Metropolitan Museum of Art has gone deeply into a field with which not everyone associates it: that of African tribal art. After having given good space and a very handsome installation to ''Treasures of Ancient Nigerian Art'' last fall, the museum has now given a much larger space - the Sackler Wing - to examples of African art from the collection of Paul and Ruth Tishman. In all, 150 objects from all over Africa are included in the show, which is called ''For Spirits and Kings,'' and an international and multiracial pool of no fewer than 71 distinguished scholars has contributed to the catalogue, which costs $35 clothbound and $14.95 in paperback.   What we see at the Metropolitan is an anthology. Hardly less various than Africa itself, it speaks for a collection that is growing fast. (Roughly half of what is on show has been acquired by the Tishmans in the last 10 years.) Where the Nigerian show was marked by a focus on antiquity and an almost palpable local pride, the Tishman collection ranges impartially from the inaccessible cliffs of the Bandiagara escarpment in the western Sudan to what the catalogue succinctly describes as ''the barren Kalahari desert, icy Mount Kilimanjaro and the lush hills of the temperate cape.'' It also includes many pieces of recent date.

headline: BRITAIN TO CUT PRICE OF OIL, RAISING HOPE OF WORLD REDUCTION
abstract: Britain, a major producer of oil from the North Sea, has agreed to cut prices by $2 a barrel, enhancing the prospect of a substantial downward move in world oil prices.   The decision, which will lower the official price to $37.25 a barrel from $39.25, will add to the already intense pressure being felt by other exporters, particularly Nigeria, Libya and Algeria, to reduce their prices in the wake of the inability of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries to reach a unified pricing agreement in Geneva 10 days ago.   Moreover, a still larger price reduction by Britain remains a possibility. Producing companies in the North Sea, principally British Petroleum and Shell, made clear that they believed the offer yesterday of a $2 reduction by the British National Oil Company, which markets most of Britain's oil, was insufficient.

headline: EXPORTS OFF FOR TOYOTA AND NISSAN
abstract: The two largest car makers in Japan, the Toyota Motor Company and the Nissan Motor Company, said yesterday that their production and their exports to the United Stattes had dropped in May from a year earlier, partly because of export restraints. headline: PRESSURE ON WORLD PRICE INTENSIFED

That is as much as $6 a barrel below prices charged by Algeria, Nigeria and Libya, the three highest-priced producers, for oil of comparable quality. headline: CRACKDOWN UNDER WAY IN SOUTH AFRICA Mol of kenya
abstract: In what amounts to the most severe crackdown by the security police since Prime Minister P.W. Botha took office nearly three years ago, about 30 black trade-union leaders and student activists have been arrested in the last three weeks under security laws permitting detention without trial.   The pattern of the arrests suggested that the security police were looking for evidence that recent black protests have been coordinated. More specifically, the police were assumed in black politicl circles to be searching for links between legal black organizations and the African National Congress, the oldest black political movement in South Africa, which has been outlawed for 21 years.   The most recent and dramatic arrests, however, involved a smaller, allegedly extremist underground movement called the South African Youth Revolutionary Council, made up of black youths who fled South Africa after a student uprising in 1976 and 1977 in Soweto, Johannesburg's black township. The council, which surfaced first in Botswana, was later reported to be receiving funds from Nigeria. More recently, it has been rumored to be getting backing from the Palestine Liberation Organization. Its activities have been shadowy, but an impression has grown that it is ready to consider terrorist tactics that have apparently been rejected by the African National Congress.

headline: AFRICAN OPEC MEMBERS REJECT OIL PRICE CUTS
abstract: The four African members of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, which charge the world's highest prices for their crude, said yesterday that they would not bow to pressure from Saudi Arabia and the international oil companies to lower their oil prices.   Oil industry officials said the decision by Libya, Algeria, Nigeria and Gabon set the stage for a showdown with the oil companies that have been buying their crude. The companies have warned the Africans to lower their oil prices, which currently range from $37 to $41 a barrel, threatening to halt oil purchases when contracts come up for renewal July 1.   The oil ministers of the four African countries met yesterday in Algiers to explore strategies for dealing with the oil glut and the severe downward pressure on world oil prices, engineered largely by Saudi Arabia.

headline: NORWAY CUTS OIL PRICE BY 10% ADDING TO PRESSURE ON AFRICANS
abstract: Norway's state-owned oil company announced yesterday that it was reducing the price of its North Sea crude oil by 10 percent, another indication of the intense downward pressure on world oil prices.   This widely expected price cut brought Norwegian crude into line with the price of Britain's North Sea oil and put additional pressure on the high-priced African oil producers to lower their prices.   Although Norway and Britain are not members of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, until now both of them had pegged their crude oil prices to those of OPEC's African members - Libya, Nigeria, Algeria and Gabon. On Tuesday these four producers vowed to hold their prices at $40 to $41 a barrel even though their oil is almost identical to the North Sea's low-sulfur crude.

headline: MOROCCO, IN REVERSAL, PROPOSES CEASE-FIRE AND VOTE FOR WESTERN SAHARA
abstract: King Hassan II of Morocco announced today that he was prepared to agree to a cease-fire in the guerrilla war in the Western Sahara and a referendum under international supervision on continued Moroccan rule there.   This statement, made at a meeting here of heads of state and government of members of the Organization of African Unity, marked a reversal of the King's refusal to accept such proposals a few months ago by a committee consisting of Nigeria, Mali, Tanzania, Guinea and the Ivory Coast.   But his remarks, while applauded by backers of the guerrillas, were denounced by representatives of the Polisario guerrilla organization, a Marxist group fighing for independence for the Western Sahara.   Ibrahim Hakim, the Polisario foreign affairs spokesman, said in a statement distributed to reporters that the King's words were ''another pernicious attempt by Morocco to legitimize its military occupation'' of the territory once known as the Spanish Sahara.

headline: NIGERIA CUTS PRICES OF OIL TO TRADERS
abstract: uf813 By THOMAS L. FRIEDMAN   In the first solid indication that any of the African oil producers might be willing to lower their prices, Nigeria has agreed to sell 100,000 barrels of oil a day at $37.50 a barrel, beginning tomorrow, to a group of Zurich-based oil traders, a Nigerian oil industry source reported yesterday.   The deal marks a discount of $2.50 a barrel from Nigeria's official contract price of $40 a barrel.  The report came a week after Nigeria, Algeria and Libya - whose oil is the highest priced among all members of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries - had said they would not drop their official prices of $40 to $41 a barrel, despite the worldwide oil glut. Holding Tough Discussions   Oil industry officials cautioned, however, that there was no indication yet that Nigeria was ready to offer a similar discount to the major oil companies, which buy most of that country's current production of 850,000 barrels a day. Representatives of the companies were said yesterday to be engaged in tough discussions with the Nigerians and with other African oil producers.

headline: OIL: NIGERIA'S MIXED BLESSING
abstract: The business of oil is all-pervasive in Nigeria, from the foreign executives eager to carve out a share of the riches to the hundreds of thousands of Nigerians who have set up beach shanties near the big cities to cash in on the oil boom.   Thus Nigeria, with its oil-based economy, is particularly vulnerable to the pressures of the current world oversupply of oil.  The surplus has already forced Nigeria's oil output down to levels below those needed to sustain the country's $125 billion, five-year development plan.   If the current surplus does not end within coming months, a Western economist warns, black Africa's economic giant could be forced to slow development projects, possibly adding to urban unemployment, and restrict imports, putting upward pressure on an already high inflation rate. Nigeria may also need to borrow overseas.

headline: OPEC APPEARS READY TO LIMIT PRICING SPREAD
abstract: In what might be a major breakthrough in the bitter OPEC dispute over oil pricing, Libya indicated today a willingness to reduce its official oil price of $40 a barrel and Saudi Arabia said it might raise its price from $32 a barrel.   Analysts said the conciliatory statements on both sides seemed to indicate the possibility of a compromise that would put official OPEC prices in a range of roughly from $33 or $34 a barrel to $37 a barrel. The current range is from the $32 for a 42-gallon barrel charged by the Saudis to the $40 charged by Libya and the two other African members of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, Nigeria and Algeria.   The new price range, if it is in fact proposed and ratified at an OPEC meeting here on Wednesday, would have little effect on the prices Americans pay for gasoline and other oil products.

headline: A BAD RAP FOR LAGOS
abstract: This West African capital may be the most maligned city in the world.  Power blackouts, traffic jams, armed robberies and murders occur in all West African cities. Why does Lagos have a reputation for being worse than all the others? Is the reason just that it is bigger, so problems happen more often and are harder to handle? Or is the reason more spiteful than that?   Nigeria, with $25 billion in oil revenue last year and a population estimated at 90 million, is the only black African nation that can aspire to be a world power in this century. Many outsiders, Westerners and Africans alike, may not like that prospect. Certainly they seem eager to believe the worst about this country and to pass it on. For 18 months, as I traveled this West African coast, people kept telling me how awful Lagos was. After six weeks here, I beg to differ.

headline: REAGAN'S MESSAGE
abstract: To the Editor:     The Reagan Administration's campaign against the Government of Libya, the United States' third largest foreign supplier of petroleum and site of substantial U.S. corporate installations, will be widely noted abroad.   v.   hatever the U.S. Navy's successful provocation of a firefight with Libyan planes may have demonstrated about the sanctity of international waterways and the wages of international terrorism, it demonstrated an important point about American foreign policy:   As much as its predecessors, Ronald Reagan's conservative, business-oriented Administration is prepared to take actions in the service of what, rightly or wrongly, it conceives to be important political and strategic goals, even when they go directly counter to major American economic interests in a third-world country.   Feisty governments as different in their orientations as Nigeria and South Africa will certainly note that providing the United States with strategic resources and courting United States investment will little avail them should their political actions run counter to some Washington Administration's view of ''responsible'' international behavior. headline: NIGERIA REDUCES CRUDE OIL PRICE BY $4 A BARREL
abstract: Nigeria, the No.2 exporter of oil to the United States, announced yesterday that it would lower the price of its oil by $4 a barrel in what may be the first in a series of price cuts by OPEC members in the face of a worldwide oil glut.   Although the immediate effect at American gasoline pumps is expected to be negligible, industry experts said that Nigeria's price reduction - to $36 from $40 - if matched by other African producers, could reduce gasoline prices in this country by two or three cents a gallon.   ''It is a remarkable and welcome development,'' said Walter J.  Levy, a prominent oil economist. headline: U.S. SIGNS TWO AID AGREEMENTS WITH NIGERIA
abstract: The United States and Nigeria today signed two technical aid accords and announced steps to improve commercial relations.   Two days of meetings between delegations headed by Vice President Alex Ekwueme of Nigeria and Vice President Bush did not, however, result in an agreement on the price of liquefied natural gas that Nigeria hopes to sell to the United States from a liquefication plant under development. The reduction, Nigeria's second in two months, was viewed by market experts as evidence that reports that OPEC members were near a compromise on a unified base price of $34 might be premature. The reason is that the Nigerian price, because of quality and transportation surcharges of up to $5 a barrel that that country usually levies, would be too low to fit in with the accord.

headline: U.S. IS CONSIDERING LOGISTICAL SUPPORT FOR FORCE IN CHAD
abstract: The United States is actively considering a request by Nigeria to provide transport and supplies for part of a 5,000-member African peacekeeping force that will be sent to Chad to replace departing Libyan troops, Administration officials said today.    After taking the lead for months in urging France and African nations to bring about the withdrawal of Libyan forces from Chad, the Reagan Administration has now been asked to play a significant role in helping put that country on its feet again economically, officials said, since Libya is cutting off all support.   Washington has agreed to participate tomorrow in a meeting in Paris of prospective aid donors, officials said, to discuss ways of saving Chad from total economic collapse. Request From Nigeria   American officials said Washington was also inclined to help Nigeria, which had asked the United States to fly a 2,000-member Nigerian contingent to Chad, and to assist other nations that asked.  But they said Washington would prefer that the official request come from the Organization of African Unity itself.

headline: A STOUT CONSTITUTION
abstract: SO PROUDLY SHE SAILED Tales of Old Ironsides.  By Olga Cabral.  Illustrated. 170 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin. $8.95.  (Ages 10 to 14)   ON the morning of Sept. 20, 1797, a large, cheerful crowd gathered around the fine new frigate that stood, bright with flags, her hull gleaming with fresh copper, ready to slide down the ways into Boston harbor. A little after noon, carpenters knocked out her shoring timbers and - nothing happened. The Constitution sullenly refused to go into the water; a glum symbol of the thousand problems besetting the infant American Navy, she stood immobile until the following month.

abstract: Several hundred more Zairian soldiers arrived in this capital today, bringing the strength of the Pan-African peacekeeping force for Chad to 700, military sources said. headline: JOHNSON PRODUCTS STRUGGLING AGAINST SMUGGLERS IN NIGERIA
abstract: Efforts of the Johnson Products Company to bolster its sagging profits by establishing an operation in Nigeria have suffered a setback from the illegal flow of its products into that country.   Smugglers have hurt Johnson Products by buying its personal grooming items cheaply in the United States and selling them in Nigeria at a lower price than the company can.   The smugglers undercut the Johnson Products price because whatever the company sells in Nigeria is manufactured in Nigeria, and the company must import the chemicals, plastic containers and other materials needed to make the items there. As a result, the company's products are more expensive in Nigeria than they are in the United States.

headline: Chad and Its Neighbors' Webs
abstract: A year ago, troops from neighboring Libya helped Chad's President Goukouni Oueddei consolidate his power. Neighboring Sudan, a target of Libyan subversion, was alarmed. Neighboring Nigeria, sensing Colonel Qaddafi's visions of empire, pressed the Organization of African Unity to protest. France and the United States, with interests of their own, moved to strengthen allies in the region. And last month, President Goukouni seemed to respond to international concerns. He arranged for an African peacekeeping force to come in.  The Libyans quickly withdrew, declaring that chaos, not peace, would follow.

headline: CANADA ARRESTS TWO ART DEALERS IN IMPORT CASE
abstract: Two Manhattan art dealers have been arrested in Canada on charges of bringing into that country a rare and ancient work of African sculpture without an export license from the Nigerian Government.  The case is believed to represent the first move by the Canadian Government to enforce a law that bars unlicensed entry of foreign cultural properties.   The two men, Ben Heller and Issaka Zango, had hoped to sell the sculpture, a 13-inch-tall terra cotta maternity figure from the Nok culture, for $650,000. But the work was confiscated by the police in Calgary and remains in police custody. A third person, Firaz Kassam, a Calgary resident acting as agent for the dealers, was also arrested.

headline: MILITARY COUP IN GHANA ALARMS WEST AFRICAN GOVERNMENTS
abstract: The military coup in Ghana last week has alarmed governments, both civilian and military, in West Africa, according to African and Western diplomats.   Moreover, according to those diplomats, the coup led by Jerry J.  Rawlings that toppled the civilian Government of President Hilla Limann underlined a trend in West Africa that began in April 1979, when President William R. Tolbert Jr. of Liberia was assassinated in a military coup engineered by Master Sgt. Samuel K. Doe. Later that year, in November, there were two other coups in this region: in Upper Volta, which had a multi-party democratic system, and in Guinea-Bissau, which had been experimenting with a multicandidate electoral program within the Marxist African Party for the Independence of Guinea and the Cape Verde Islands.   Mr. Rawlings's coup, in which he seized power for the second time in two years, is also likely to be a setback for the United States and other Western powers, according to the diplomats, who point to the increasingly bitter anti-Western statements by the former Ghanaian Air Force flight lieutenant in recent months. Mr. Rawlings contended that ''insidious Western interests'' were as much responsible for the high degree of corruption in Ghana as the greed of members of President Limann's ruling People's National Party.

headline: YOUNG TAKES OATH AS ATLANTA MAYOR
abstract: Andrew Jackson Young became Atlanta's 55th Mayor tonight in inauguration ceremonies where he reminded several thousand cheering supporters of Atlanta's leading role in integration and the election of blacks and said tha t the city ''must point the way in theeconomic aren a as it has in social and political spheres.''   Mr. Young, the city's second black Mayor, said the ''challenge of the 80's is economic'' on a ''planet that is vulnerable to cataclysmic wealth and resource maldistribution.''   He also called for ''a new consciousness of Atlanta as a regional center of international finance and export trade.'' As if to underscore his determination to take the city along new paths, he introduced visitors to the ceremonies such as representatives from Liberia and Nigeria, the Secretary General of the Organization of African Unity and a former foreign minister of Panama.

headline: AFRICAN FORCES IN CHAD SEEN SHIFTING ROLE
abstract: The Organization of African Unity's peacekeeping force in Chad is trying to redeploy forces and is seeking reinforcements to meet a potential new threat from a rebellious former Defense Minister, according to Western and Nigerian military sources here.   The former official, Hissen Habre, has made wide gains in the east of the country after last November's withdrawal of Libyan troops.  The redeployment of the peacekeeping force, which involves some United States logistic support, implies a subtle shift in its approach to its mission, the sources said. Previously, the African army, which is composed of contingents from Nigeria, Senegal and Zaire, perceived itself as a neutral buffer between Chad's many warring factions, principally those of Mr. Habre and President Goukouni Oueddei.

headline: AFRICAN AIDES DISCUSS SAHARA AT KENYA PARLEY
abstract: Nine African foreign ministers met here today to discuss the Western Sahara, where an Algerian-supported guerrilla organization known as the Polisario Front has been fighting Morocco for more than six years.   The foreign ministers, from Tanzania, Sierra Leone, Nigeria, the Sudan, Guinea, Mali, Algeria, Morocco and Kenya, are expected to prepare an agenda for about a dozen African heads of state who are scheduled to attend a conference here starting Monday. The heads of state are to discuss the Western Sahara question as well as the Organization of African Unity's peacekeeping force in Chad.

headline: PEACE FORCE IN CHAD FACING A FUND SHORTAGE
abstract: The Organization of African Unity was told today at a special meeting here that it could no longer afford to maintain a peacekeeping force in Chad unless new emergency financial donations were forthcoming.   The secretary general of the organization, Edem Kodjo of Togo, said that it would cost $163 million to maintain troops in Chad over the next year. President Daniel arap Moi of Kenya, the current chairman of the O.A.U., appealed to the organization's members and to the international community at large for fresh funds for the support of the troops from Nigeria, Senegal and Zaire that are now in Chad. The strength of the force is estimated at 3,000.

headline: CHAD REBEL IS SAID TO WEIGH ATTACK
abstract: Chad's rebellious former Defense Minister, Hissen Habre, says he will attack toward the capital, Ndjamena, if the Organization of African Unity does not make progress toward a settlement in the war-ravaged land, according to reports reaching here from eastern Chad.   The reports, quoted by Western diplomatic sources, said Mr. Habre was theatening to move within the next few weeks. A committee of the Organization of African Unity is currently meeting in Nairobi, Kenya, to discuss Chad and other issues.   Mr. Habre, the sources said, spoke of his plans to visitors at his headquarters in eastern Chad in recent weeks and details of these conversations are now reaching Khartoum.

headline: POPE STARTS WEST AFRICA TRIP TODAY
abstract: Nine months after an assassin's bullets nearly took his life, Pope John Paul II will resume his travels Friday with an seven-day, four-nation journey to West Africa.   Originally planned to cover only Nigeria and Gabon, the Pope's itinerary has been extended to include two small countries that occasioned surprise when the schedule was announced last month.   On his way from Lagos, Nigeria, to Libreville, Gabon, on Wednesday, the Pope will stop for six hours in Cotonou, the capital of Benin, formally known as Dahomey. And on the following Friday the Pope will visit the two main towns of Equatorial Guinea, Malabo on Bioko Island, which in Spanish colonial days was Santa Isabel on Fernando Po, and Bata in Rio Muni, the mainland part of the small country on the Atlantic Ocean.

headline: O.A.U. SAYS IT WILL PULL OUT FORCE UNLESS CHAD AND REBELS HALT WAR
abstract: The Organization of African Unity said today that it would withdraw its peacekeeping forces from Chad by June 30 unless President Goukouni Oueddei arranged a cease-fire and started negotiating with rebels who are trying to overthrow his Government.   In a resolution unanimously approved by leaders of 11 African nations, Mr. Goukouni was also told that he must organize legislative and presidential elections by June 30 and fashion a new constitution for his country, which has been swept by civil war almost since its independence from France 22 years ago.   The Chadian President walked out of the session early this morning and was quoted by participants as shouting, ''I am betrayed!'' Later, after the O.A.U. had announced its decision, Mr. Goukouni's spokesman, Ramati al-Khaly, said that the Chadian Government rejected the resolution. ''We took no part in the conference and we are not bound by its resolutions,'' he said. ''We contest the legality of this O.A.U. committee.''

headline: SUDAN IS SKEPTICAL ABOUT O.A.U.'S ROLE
abstract: President Gaafar al-Nimeiry said today that he did not believe the Organization of African Unity's peacekeeping force in Chad was able to ''stop war by military means''and he called Chad's President, Goukouni Oueddei, an obstacle to peace.   General Nimeiry also said in an interview that Libya's pullout from Chad in November was a ''tactical withdrawal'' that had not ended ''the Libyan danger to the Sudan and Africa.''   The Sudanese leader indirectly accused Ethiopia of failing to reach a political settlement with Eritrean separatists and said that the Sudan would be affected by a reported new Ethiopian military push against the Eritreans near the Sudanese border.   General Nimeiry gave the interview in his office at Friendship Hall, a Chinese-built edifice in central Khartoum. The conversation coincided with an O.A.U. meeting in Nairobi, Kenya, at which the fate of the peace force in Chad is under discussion.

headline: POPE GETS EXUBERANT GREETING IN NIGERIA
abstract: Greeted with exuberance by huge crowds in black Africa's most populous city, Pope John Paul II today began an eight-day journey to four West African nations.   ''For me this is a moment of joy,'' the Pope said in responding to the airport greeting by President Shehu Shagari. ''Before me there unfolds a vision of hope.''   The 61-year-old John Paul stepped off the plane after a five-and-ahalf-hour flight from Rome, his first trip outside Italy since he was shot last May. The joy that he expressed seemed deeply felt on the first stop of the journey, which will also take him to Benin, Gabon and Equatorial Guinea before he returns to Rome next Friday.

headline: POPE TO NIGERIANS: DEFEND THE FAMILY
abstract: Pope John Paul II said mass today for hundreds of thousands of Nigerian Catholics at the outskirts of this city, which was a battleground that changed hands many times during the country's civil war.   The crowd, mostly Ibo tribesmen from this province in eastern Nigeria that briefly seceded to form the independent nation of Biafra, overflowed with enthusiasm when the Pope, on the first full day of his African journey, landed in a helicopter.   The people chanted, danced and waved paper papal flags of yellow and white and Nigerian ones in green and white. The bitter civil war that put down the secession is forgotten, former Biafrans said, and no one referred to it.

headline: JOHN PAUL, IN NIGERIA, ENCOUNTERS POLES
abstract: Pope John Paul II was greeted by several hundred Poles, waving flags and singing Polish hymns, as he rode in an open car today through multitudes of Nigerians who had flocked here to celebrate mass with him.   The Pope signaled his driver to stop, leaned over and kissed a homemade Polish flag held toward him by 12-year-old Peter Krzeski, the son of a Pole working in Nigeria. In an equally spontaneous gesture, Peter hugged the flag to his chest.   As the driver made to start up again, the group of 300 to 400 Poles, many of whom claimed membership in a Nigeria chapter of Solidarity, the once-free trade union, broke into an ancient hymn that links Polish patriotism and Roman Catholicism, ''God Save Poland.''

headline: JOHN PAUL ASSURES AFRICANS OF RESPECT FOR THEIR VALUES
abstract: Pope John Paul II preached today, the fourth day of his pilgrimage to Africa, on the Roman Catholic Church's respect for the many cultures of this world.   ''The church comes to bring Christ,'' he said in a speech to Nigerian bishops. ''It does not come to bring the cultures of another race.''   Vatican specialists on African affairs depict the Pope as concerned over how to integrate Catholicism into African cultures at a time when the people of developing countries are becoming increasingly aware of their own cultural values and less eager than in the colonial past to accept unquestioningly the values and practices of alien cultures.

headline: POPE ASSERTS OF POLAND, 'I DO NOT LOSE HOPE'
abstract: Pope John Paul II told the Polish community here, in the presence of the ambassador of the martial law regime of Gen. Wojciech Jaruzelski, that he remained hopeful that the prayers of the Polish people would be answered.   Speaking circumspectly and mostly indirectly at a reception for his countrymen, the Pope left no doubt that he meant Polish desires for a return to normality and an end to martial law.   He said he spoke as a son of a people that had been sorely tested through the centuries, had had to contend with powerful neighbors and had had to fight ''for your freedom and ours.'' The phrase was the motto of the members of a Polish legion that fought under Napoleon's command against Russia, Prussia and Austria in the hope that a French victory would restore their country's independence after its partition among the three powers.

headline: MEXICO'S ROAD TO TROUBLE IS COATED WITH OIL (1975-81)
abstract: When Mexico discovered large new oil reserves in the late 1970's, it vowed to avoid the mistakes of other third-world energy exporters that had allowed oil to dominate and distort their economies, sometimes with disastrous political results.   Iran's experience, which culminated in the ouster of the Shah, was the freshest warning. Mexican officials also took note of Venezuela's reliance on food imports, Nigeria's ports clogged with foreign goods and Saudi Arabia's enterprises overrun by foreign technicians.   Yet, almost fatefully, Mexico has also become addicted to oil, its dependence suddenly exposed by the world glut. Earning less from exports and borrowing more abroad than it had planned, the Government last week was forced to devalue the peso. The Bank of Mexico stopped intervening on exchange markets and the currency immediately lost 30 percent of its value.

headline: OPEC SETS REVIEW OF OIL MARKET
abstract: The president of OPEC, reacting in part to Britain's big cut in its oil prices on Tuesday, said today that the oil group would hold a consultative meeting this month to discuss the effect on prices of a worldwide oversupply of oil, according to reports from Abu Dhabi.   ''I hope countries which are thinking about reducing their prices will wait, because we are determined to find the solutions which will help these countries and other countries,'' the official, Sheik Mani Said al-Otaiba, told reporters in Abu Dhabi. headline: Correspondents' Choice
abstract: Portugal The Algarve's unhurried pace   Portugal's southern Algarve coast may be Europe's last uncluttered and inexpensive but civilized vacation site. Shielded by hills from the cold air of northern Europe, the Algarve enjoys African weather all year round and claims more sunshine than any other European resort. From June until October, a scorching blanket of dry heat settles over the coast, with its immense sandy beaches, its tiny smugglers' coves and its crumbling cliffs of golden stone, honeycombed by wind and tide. The pace of life is African too, with peasant women swathed in black driving mule carts down narrow lanes and barefoot fishermen mending nets on the beaches. To reach the Algarve, fly direct to the international airport at Faro, Portugal's southernmost city, or take an air-conditioned bus from Lisbon. Once there, you will need a car; Hertz, Avis and Europacar have offices at the airport and in most of the coastal towns. Many visitors rent villas, but if that is impractical, stay at a pousada, one of the Government-owned inns that are clean, comfortable and often spectacularly beautiful. There are two on the Algarve. The more dramatically situated is the pousada at Sagres, on the cliffs at Europe's most southwesterly point. The other, in an old monastery, is up in the hills at Sao Bras de Alportel. Both have excellent restaurants but are small, so reserve in advance. The road running eastward from Sagres passes through the old whitewashed port of Lagos, from which Henry the Navigator's ships set out to explore Africa and Latin America.

headline:
Dance;
EMELIN ENDS SEASON WITH TWO GROUPS
abstract:
THE Emelin Theater in Mamaroneck will present two unusual dance events next weekend. To close the theater's dance series this season, the Dinizulu African Dancers, Drummers and Singers will offer a program of songs and dances from South Africa, Nigeria, Ghana and Sierra Leone at 8:30 P.M. Saturday. And next Sunday afternoon, the Windemere Ballet Company will celebrate its 15th anniversary with a 2 P.M. performance.

For more than 30 years, Nana Yao Opare Dinizulu - Nana is a Ghanaian title of respect meaning chief - has led the oldest continuing African dance company in the United States, bringing the colorful performance to audiences here and in Africa. The Dinizulu program will include the spectacular narrative dances and music of the authentic African repertoire. Many of the works tell a story that is narrated during the performance. One such piece from South Africa is ''Ibutho,'' a dance in two sections depicting warriors in battle and the women who await them at home. The company is made up of American and native African performers.

headline: OIL-PRICE DROP PUTS SQUEEZE ON LENDING TO POOR NATIONS
abstract: WASHINGTON THE moon has its dark side, and so does the slide in world oil prices. Although it has already led to lower inflation in the United States and other oil-importing countries and might help boost them out of recession, the drop in oil prices could also cause further tightening in international lending, especially to the more impoverished countries of the third world.   Even some third world oil exporters have been caught in the squeeze. Nigeria, a heavy borrower which has been running a monthly trade deficit of $600 million, last week froze virtually all imports because of the decline in its oil revenues. The most populous African country with nearly 100 million inhabitants, it is under pressure to cut prices more deeply than permitted by OPEC agreements to try to increase sales and revenues. Acting in support of Nigeria - and the oil cartel's $34-a-barrel benchmark price - Saudi Arabia and Kuwait have threatened to cancel contracts with international oil companies that reduce purchases of Nigeria's $36.50-a-barrel oil in favor of equally high-grade $31 oil from the North Sea and other non-OPEC sources. Saudi Arabia also is reportedly extending emergency credits to Nigeria to keep it from breaking ranks with the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries on prices.

headline: FLAMES OF ISLAMIC FERVOR UNSETTLE NIGERIA'S NORTH

Among the slogans they painted on campus buildings was one that read, ''Down with the American system.''   Among the demonstrators, student leaders said, were many Islamic fundamentalists, young people calling for a revolution that will purge what they deem to be a corruption of the religion among the traditional hierarchy in the vast reaches of northern Nigeria. The fundamentalists belong to a sect known as ''Izala,'' a name that, according to a scholar of Islam here, means ''the sweeping away of heretical innovations.''   Islamic fundamentalism is one of many strains and tensions spreading across northern Nigeria in the period before elections next year that will determine whether or not President Shehu Shagari gets a second term. A diplomat based in the area compared the varying strands of the politics here to ''a pile of cracked records placed on top of each other so that you never know where the next crack will appear or how one fissure affects another.''

headline: DIPLOMAT'S CHARGES FOCUS OF INQUIRIES
abstract:
TRENTON ALTHOUGH the State Department and a member of the Congressional Black Caucus are pressing for full disclosure, some New Jersey officials say that the results of a State Police investigation of charges made by a Nigerian diplomat may never be fully known.

The diplomat, Ngam Nwachuku, Senior First Secretary in the Nigerian Mission to the United Nations, said that last Feb. 27, after he had tried to get directions from a trooper parked on the shoulder of I-287 in Middlesex County, he and his wife were dragged from their car and taken to the State Police barracks in Edison.

In the next two and a half hours, Mr. Nwachuku said, two troopers repeatedly called him a ''nigger,'' handcuffed him and his wife and ransacked their Mercedes-Benz while they stood outside in the cold with their 2 1/2-year-old son.

Mr. Nwachuku said that they were finally released when a sergeant realized who they were and ''apologized.'' The State Police will not comment, even though its Internal Affairs Department has finished its investigation. A police spokesman, Lieut. Joseph B. Kobus, said that the report would be discussed only by Attorney General Irwin Kimmelman, who is reviewing its findings.
