headline: MUSIC, MUGGINGS AND A CURE FOR CANCER
abstract:
ARDABIOLA A Fantasy. By Yevgeny Yevtushenko. Translated by Armorer Wason. 123 pp. New York: St. Martin's Press. $11.95.

YEVGENY YEVTUSHENKO, the most newsworthy living Russian poet, has written here a short, entertaining novel. It is set in the Soviet Union, has excellent local color and may well appeal to American readers wishing to sample modern Muscovy from a safe distance. The delights of traveling in a packed Moscow tram, the thrills of a Siberian wake and even the joys of changing a naughty Soviet infant's diaper in midair halfway between the two - such topics are adroitly handled. Themes include research into the effect of music on plant growth, muggings by Soviet skinheads with bicycle chains, orgies of vodka swilling, and ecological lamentations. It follows that no one is likely, after reading this book, to feel that the Soviet Union has been entirely left behind by 20th-century progress.

headline: WOLE SOYINKA: WRITING, AFRICA AND POLITICS
abstract:
WOLE SOYINKA, the Nigerian playwright, novelist, poet and essayist, is Africa's best-known writer. He is also one of that continent's most controversial social critics. Several times Mr. Soyinka has gone into hiding or fled Nigeria to avoid reprisals for his criticisms of Government policies. He was twice jailed for political activities, once in 1965 and again in 1967-69, when, as he grimly recounts in his 1972 book, ''The Man Died,'' he was tortured and held in solitary confinement for two years.

Mr. Soyinka, who will be 51 years old next month, was born in Abeokuta, in the Yoruba region of southwestern Nigeria. He was educated at Government College in Ibadan and at the University of Leeds in Yorkshire, England. In 1958-59 he was play reader at the Royal Court Theater in London and soon after returned to Nigeria. He is chairman of the theater arts department at the University of Ife, in Ile-Ife, Nigeria. His latest book is a childhood memoir, ''Ake,'' chosen by The New York Times Book Review as one of the 12 best books of 1982. ''A Play of Giants,'' his most recent dramatic work, is a satire on African dictators. It received its world premiere last year at the Yale Repertory Theater in New Haven, where this interview took place.

headline: OPEC OIL MINISTERS MEET AMID DISCORD ON PRICING POLICY
abstract: OPEC oil ministers assembled here today for a critical meeting after weeks of informal discussions apparently failed to yield any agreement on how to strengthen their organization, according to officials arranging the meeting for Friday.   Saudi Arabia and its Persian Gulf allies have been urging other members of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries to cut oil prices, stick to agreed production levels and perhaps reduce output a bit this summer.   All of this would constitute an effort to re-establish OPEC's control of the world oil market at a time when demand is falling and production by its members is on the rise.      Some Members Unconvinced    At emergency talks in Algiers last weekend, however, the oil ministers of Kuwait and Venezuela failed to convince those of Algeria, Libya and Nigeria of the need for an oil price cut, according to the OPEC officials. Algeria, Libya and Nigeria believe a cut would discriminate against them, making their oil relatively harder to sell.

headline: THE WONDERS OF AFRICAN ART EXPLORED IN 2 EXHIBITIONS
abstract: JUST by happenstance, two noteworthy shows of African art have opened this week, at two different institutions. They're interesting not only for their subject matter, which is engrossing enough (and not unrelated), but also because they illustrate two very different approaches - one traditional, the other innovative - to the presentation of work that is at once art and anthropology. The traditional presentation is ''The Art of Cameroon'' at the American Museum of Natural History, Central Park West at 79th Street (through Oct. 15), and the innovative one - as might be guessed from the title - is ''Sets, Series and Ensembles in African Art,'' at the Center for African Art, 54 East 68th Street (through Oct. 20).   The Cameroon show is a dazzling display of ''royal'' art, focusing on the Grassfields area of what is known officially today as the United Republic of Cameroon, in west central Africa. With one of the continent's richest art traditions, the Grassfields - a high, verdant plateau that borders on Nigeria - is a complex of tribal chiefdoms, each ruled by a hereditary king or Fon together with a group of titled dignitaries. The tribal art, as explained in the show's handsome catalogue by Tamara Northern, curator of ethnographic art at Dartmouth College's Hood Museum, was primarily made for the Fon and his nobles, and is intended to express their power and prestige.

headline: NEW & NOTEWORTHY
abstract: LYING IN BED, by Mark Harris. (McGraw-Hill, $6.95.) Mark Harris's 11th novel is a series of letters between an impotent novelist-professor and a multitude of people. In 1984 Jerome Charyn remarked here that if the book ''is scratchy and verbose, it is also extravagantly funny and sad. . . . a squawky story about the telling of stories, a long, playful epistle to readers and writers.'' COLETTE, by Joanna Richardson. (Laurel/Dell, $4.95.) Colette, who died in 1954, lived 81 years. She was France's most famous female author, and even had a brief career as a dancer, mime and actress. Reviewers said in 1984 that while Joanna Richardson tells all about the writer's scandals, she does so without making a scandal of the biography. Because so many Parisian authors had something to say about Colette, the book has been described as a ripe and witty anthology of modern French criticism. Miss Richardson has a great subject, one reviewer said, and does not waste a single nuance. DOUBLE YOKE, by Buchi Emecheta. (George Braziller, $5.95.) Buchi Emecheta is a Nigerian-born writer who has lived in England since 1962 and who will be teaching at Harvard University this fall. This, her seventh novel, is about two students - one female, one male - at a Nigerian university. Their mutual love is tested by their conflicts with Nigerian society's traditional views of male and female roles. headline: Nigeria
abstract: Geography With an area of 356,700 square miles, Nigeria is about the size of California, Nevada and Arizona combined. Its name derives from that of the Niger River, the third-longest river in Africa, and its territory ranges from southern coastal swamps to tropical forests, from open woodlands, grass and savannas to semidesert in the far north. Nigeria, which is relatively flat, has rich oil and mineral deposits. Population Nigeria's population, estimated to range from 80 million to 95 million, includes some 250 tribal groups. About half the people are Moslems, primarily in the north. There are many Christians in the south. English is the official language but major African languages, such as Hausa, Yoruba and Ibo, are widely used. About 70 percent of the population is illiterate. Economy Nigeria is one of the largest suppliers of oil to the United States. It must import 70 percent of its food and raw materials. In addition to oil, which accounts for more than 90 percent of its foreign exchange, Nigeria also exports cocoa and rubber.

headline:

A DIFFERENT PATH TO THE U.S. OPEN
abstract:
The story of Akeem Abdul Olajuwon's introduction to basketball is now an integral part of sports lore: A coach is traveling along a road in Nigeria when he eyes two teams playing soccer. One of them has a goalie who is at least 7 feet tall. Slamming on the brakes, the coach gets out and asks the kid if he has ever dunked a basketball. The rest, as they say, is history.

''I averaged three goals a match in high school and was a good center-forward. But because I was so good, a lot of people kicked me, and I got tripped a lot. I got kicked so bad, I said, 'Forget it.' headline: STAGE: 'FABIOLA,' TALE OF FAMILY AND CASTRO
abstract: ANY play that reduces the Cuban revolution to a tale of squabbling in-laws and homosexual incest must have something going for it - even if that something is mainly bad taste. In ''Fabiola,'' a new potboiler at the Theater for the New City, the writer Eduardo Machado fiddles madly and at times divertingly while Havana burns. ''Fabiola'' purports to deal with such matters as the rise of Castro, the collapse of the Bay of Pigs invasion and the horrors of totalitarianism. The evening is at its liveliest, however, when we watch two brothers make out feverishly in their bedroom while others fight the revolution (or counter-revolution) off stage.   As trash, this evening has its heavybreathing moments, but surely Mr. Machado, a young playwright of talent, wanted to achieve much more. ''Fabiola'' is the middle work in an ambitious trilogy whose other components have previously been staged to tantalizing effect at the Ensemble Studio Theater. All three plays tell of the same Cuban family, named Marquez, whom we follow from the backwater provinces of 1928 (''The Modern Ladies of Guanabacoa'') to Los Angeles exile in 1979 (''Broken Eggs''). Because ''Fabiola'' covers the most tumultuous period in both Marquez and Cuban history, 1955-67, one had every reason to hope that it would be the most fully realized chapter of a potentially epic saga.

headline: ART: EXHIBIT INTRODUCES ABAKANOWICZ OF POLAND
abstract: THE room is packed with rows of bodies seated on the floor, but all we see is their brown, wrinkled backs as they sit hunched over in submissive silence. They could be gulag inmates, assembled for the order of the day, or primitive tribesmen in thrall to a charismatic leader. At once individuals and a crowd, they hypnotize the viewer by virtue of their rhythmic massing.   Actually, these thin, hollowed shapes are made of burlap molded with glue by Magdalena Abakanowicz, a Polish artist whose innovative sculptural uses of cloth and fiber have not gone unmarked around the world (in 1980, she represented Poland at the Venice Biennale; in 1982, a big Abakanowicz retrospective was mounted by the Museum of Contemporary Art in Chicago). Now Abakanowicz is having her first solo show in New York, at the Xavier Fourcade Gallery, 36 East 75th Street (through Oct. 12). Odd that it hasn't happened sooner, since it's one of the more compelling exhibitions you'll see this season.

headline: SADE'S 2D ALBUM, A REFINED FUSION
abstract: ''PROMISE'' (Epic/Portrait), the second album by the Nigerian-born British pop star Sade, marks an impressive leap forward for the singer-lyricist whose debut album, ''Diamond Life,'' was a worldwide hit this year. Like its forerunner, ''Promise'' ignores the prevailing pop trend toward bright electronic surfaces in favor of a refined, acoustically based fusion of pop, jazz, funk and Latin influences. The arrangements feature horns, brass, guitar and occasional strings set against rich polyrhythmic underpinnings that suggest a funkified extension of Steely Dan's groundbreaking rock-jazz.   On ''Promise,'' even more strongly than on ''Diamond Life,'' the 25-year-old singer projects the personality of a self-possessed young cosmopolite who is precociously wise in the ways of the city. Sade's dark, vibratoless alto evokes the young Nina Simone and Astrud Gilberto filtered through American soul singers, most notably Marvin Gaye. Harmonically and rhythmically, the songs on ''Promise'' are more jazz oriented than those on ''Diamond Life.'' The melodies by Stuart Matthewman, Sade's principal collaborator, who plays guitar and saxophone in her band, keep to minor keys, enhancing the music's mood of cool, distanced melancholy.

headline: After OPEC
abstract: It's official: Once-mighty OPEC has abandoned its struggle to prop up oil prices. If members expand output as much as oil analysts anticipate, the price of a barrel could soon fall by as much as $10 from the current $28 OPEC benchmark.   That would be just desert for a greedy cartel, as well as a striking lesson in the capacity of the industrialized world to resist economic strangulation. But a collapse in oil prices would not be unalloyed good news. It could lull us into again accepting dependence on imported energy. And it certainly promises a new shock to the economies of poor oil-producing nations like Mexico, Indonesia and Nigeria. Unless importing nations act to secure the benefits, the decline in oil prices could prove almost as harmful as the steep increases of a decade ago.

headline: OPEC COMES TO GRIPS WITH A BUYER'S MARKET
abstract: Leaders of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries said last week in Geneva that they were willing to risk an all-out price war, a desperate move, to check the steep decline in sales and revenues of recent years. Since 1979, the world has needed less oil than the producing countries wanted to sell, and the resulting glut has weighed heavily on the revenues of most of OPEC's 13 members. Some, such as Nigeria, are in deep financial trouble, while others, such as Saudi Arabia, are eating into enormous treasuries piled up during the 1970's.   The leaders' aggressive stance in Geneva panicked some oil traders, sending prices for some types of oil down more than 12 percent before they recovered slightly at week's end. However, what the traders thought might be a first round in a bitter price war looked to many experts in the industry like posturing that reflected the frustrations of OPEC's leaders. ''What we have seen so far doesn't really affect our outlook,'' said Charles Franckle, chief economist for First City National Bank of Houston, which holds many loans to Southwesterners dependent on the oil industry. ''We wouldn't expect to know before next spring whether there would be anything like a price war.''

headline: NIGERIAN RULERS ASK SUPPORT FOR 'MILITARY DEMOCRACY'
abstract: The military Government announced this week that the country would return to civilian rule by Oct. 1, 1990, after an extended national debate over what its political future should look like.   Although the military's decision to remain in power for at least four more years surprised many Nigerians, the Government, in a stark departure from past Nigerian governments' practice, has declared that it will actively seek the approval of its decisions from the country's citizens in what one newspaper called a ''military democracy.''   Nigeria's President, Maj. Gen. Ibrahim Babangida, said his Government ''will not stay a day longer than is absolutely necessary,'' and added:   ''It should by now be clear to all that this administration is firmly set on a course of government by consultation with the people.'' 'A New Political Order'    In an address to the nation on Monday from Abuja, General Babangida called on Nigerians to help ''search for a new political order'' that would result in Nigeria's being ''prosperous, humanist and stable.'' That political order, he emphasized, must be rooted in Nigeria's political and economic history and not simply a ''regurgitation of the political models of the so-called advanced countries of the world.'' At the same time, General Babangida hastened to point out that the call to political debate did not mean that the ban on political parties had been lifted.

headline: U.S. BANKS FACING OIL PRICE SQUEEZE
abstract: With the plunge in oil prices to under $20 a barrel, American banks stand to suffer, especially those in Texas and New York.   Hardest hit, analysts say, will be the heavy lenders to Mexico, Venezuela, Nigeria and other countries that produce oil. The ability of those countries to service foreign debts would be severely impaired if prices do not rebound soon.   A list of such lenders includes some of the largest financial institutions in America. Citibank, for instance, is estimated to have a combined exposure to Mexico and Venezuela of $4.2 billion, equal to more than half the bank's net worth. The Manufacturers Hanover Trust Company, another big player in the international financial markets, has made an estimated $3 billion in loans to the two countries, roughly equal to its net worth.

headline: NIGERIA'S ECONOMY FACES NEW BURDEN
abstract: Nigeria's economy, already struggling with a staggering foreign debt, failing industries and a stumbling agricultural sector, faces even harder times with the sudden collapse of oil prices last week, according to economists here.   With oil making up more than 96 percent of the country's export earnings last year, the fall in oil prices is certain to have a profound effect on the new Government's ability to put into effect many much-needed programs in rural Nigeria.   Just three weeks ago Nigeria's president, Maj. Gen. Ibrahim B. Babangida, who took power in a coup last August, announced a $15.6 billion austerity budget intended to begin restructuring his nation's economy. At the time, the budget won measured praise from private economists and international bankers despite the Government's decision not to accept an International Monetary Fund loan and the accompanying restrictions on its economy. Impact on Revenue Estimates    But the drastic drop in oil prices that occurred last week has essentially decimated the Government's revenue estimates for this year, according to Western economists. North Sea Brent, the grade of crude oil that is most similar to Nigeria's Bonny light, fell to $17.25 a barrel for deliveries in April.

headline: ROCKETS' OLAJUWON FINDS SHORTEST PATH TO STARDOM
abstract: THE DREAM looks splendid, as if he has emerged from some fashion spread in a men's magazine. But this is the hallway that leads to the Houston Rockets' dressing room at the Summit, not a photographer's studio. On this night, his olive suit is neatly pressed and businesslike, and his loafers look like buttersoft Italian leather. He is smiling; the Dream always smiles.   Why? Because he loves the game, he says. Simple. Akeem Olajuwon, the gifted young Rocket center, has always played with an obvious joy, from his days as an undergraduate at the University of Houston to now. And he is not yet at the pinnacle.   Few players have adapted to the pro game more quickly than Olajuwon, known as Akeem the Dream since his college days. He did not learn the game until he was a 15-year-old youth growing up in his native Nigeria, yet today, eight years later, he is almost unanimously regarded as the league's best young center. No, the title does not belong to Patrick Ewing.

headline: An Oil-Import Tax Would be a Mistake
abstract:
The sudden drop in oil prices has set off a clamor for the United States to slap a stiff tax on imported petroleum. The proponents of an import fee as high as $12 a barrel argue that it would reduce dependence on the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, prop up domestic production and raise revenue that could be used to trim the budget deficit. They contend that only Arab producers would be hurt.

Such a program would have serious drawbacks. Obviously, American consumers and industry would lose some of the benefits of lower energy costs. More important, to the extent that foreign producers were forced to lower prices in response to a drop in American demand, an import fee would seriously damage foreign oil exporters and American oil companies with overseas properties. Some countries might consider a tariff a form of protectionism meriting retaliation.

headline: Nigeria's New Face Has His Ear to the Ground
abstract: Barely a month after seizing power in a quietly managed coup, Nigeria's new President, Maj. Gen. Ibrahim B. Babangida, was reviewing the troops during independence day celebrations. As it happened, it was raining, and the soldiers arrayed before him were drenched. So was the President. ''If my boys stand in the rain, so do I,'' he is reported to have said.   That gesture was welcomed by Nigerians who had endured 20 months of rigorously autocratic military rule under another major general. And since that rainy October day, General Babangida, the sixth military man to take over the government since independence 25 years ago, has continued down a path that is a clear departure from that of his predecessors. Again and again during the last five months, the General, a bearish man regarded as a hard worker who is quick to laugh, has put his ear to the ground to hear what his citizens are saying: Do they want to borrow money from the International Monetary Fund? Do they want to return to civilian rule and, if so, in what form? Where should the country's foreign policy head?

headline: NO THRONE, BUT KING HOLDS COURT IN YORUBA LAND
abstract: A swath of torn roadway elbows through the thinning rain forest here, hooking through a few reddish mud-walled buildings that cling precariously to its edges.   Where the road veers north, a clutter of cement buildings in pastels of yellow and pink huddle amid dark, tin-roofed houses. Here reigns the Ogiyan of Ejigbo, the king of this part of Yoruba land and one of the hundreds of traditional rulers, or obas, who continue to exercise influence over the material and spiritual lives of rural Nigerians.   ''It is heritage,'' said the Ogiyan, Omowonuola Oyeyode, settling into a brown Naugahyde armchair behind a linoleum-topped tea table on an Oriental rug. ''Traditional rulers are the foundation of Nigeria and indeed of Africa. It is my role to lead my people.'' Seated on grass mats to the Ogiyan's right, several local chiefs in brilliantly colored robes lounged against a palace wall, part of the royal retinue. As each chief arrived, he momentarily prostrated himself on the pale blue mats before the Ogiyan. To the ruler's left, retainers, their heads shaved, sat, some dozing in the humid heat.

headline: IN CHAOTIC NIGERIA, BREAD AND ROADBLOCKS ENDURE
abstract: Toward evening, just before the day's heat begins its reluctant nocturnal retreat, the bread ladies come out.   Along four-lane paved boulevards, at bus depots squeezed onto patches of hard-packed mouse-brown dirt and among squatting cassava and yam sellers at little markets, the bread ladies, like a ships gracefully slicing through churning water, glide along with golden brown loaves of bread stacked on their heads like so many blocks of wood.   They are a welcome sight here, reassuring signs that despite economic woes and political maelstroms, there is still something that endures, the certainty of bread.   That constancy shuddered a bit recently with a surge in bread prices that seemed to augur the beginnings of a nationwide bread shortage. Prices began their spurt soon after Flour Mills of Nigeria Ltd., the main flour mill in the country, announced it was shutting down for three weeks because it could not import wheat.

headline: OPEC PRODUCTION EXPECTED TO FALL
abstract: Crude oil production by the 13 members of OPEC is expected to average 800,000 barrels a day less in the first three months of this year than in the last quarter of 1985, the International Energy Agency said today. Analysts said the cutbacks by Iran and Libya were the only ones with an apparent political motive.

headline: OPEC MINISTERS TO MEET AMID GROWING DISPUTE
abstract: This weekend's emergency session of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries in Geneva is expected to be dominated by a bitter dispute between Saudi Arabia, the group's most powerful and influential producer, and an alliance of African members supported by Iran.   The 13-member group has been operating since December under the Saudi strategy of unrestrained production to depress prices and win a larger worldwide market share for its oil.   But Algeria and Libya, with the support of tiny Gabon and some non-OPEC nations in Africa, such as Angola, have grown increasingly restive, as dwindling oil prices wipe out badly needed revenues.   This week Nigeria added its voice to the dissidents. Its oil minister, Rilwanu Lukman, said he would join other African states in urging production restraint as a means of working toward average prices of $22 or $23 a barrel. Crude prices have plummeted more than 50 percent since late last year, to below $15 a barrel.

headline: POETIC VOICES SING OF BLACK LIFE IN AFRICA AND ENGLAND
abstract: Musicians and storytellers have always maintained a special position as court historians and social critics in West Africa. In modern Nigerian literary circles, the most notable writer is Wole Soyinka, whose prison poems and odes to soldiers and corrupt bureaucrats are legendary. But his fame is far outstripped by Africa's most celebrated and controversial musician, Fela Anikulapo Kuti, the creator of a style called Afro-Beat and the epitome of what Nigerians refer to as indiscipline.   Mr. Kuti, who is currently residing in a Nigerian jail on a currency smuggling conviction, has a reputation of being a flamboyant thorn in the side of Nigeria's Government, especially the country's occasional military rulers. In fact, Amnesty International has charged that Mr. Kuti's political lyrics and unorthodox behavior may have led to his arrest in September 1984, rather than his attempt to carry some $1,800 out of Nigeria en route to America for a tour. An Amnesty International report dated January 1985 stated, ''In these circumstances his guilt has not been adequately proved.''

headline: OPEC MINISTERS REJECT LIBYA APPEAL
abstract: The Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries today rejected an appeal by Libya for an oil embargo against the United States, but eight of the group's 13 members voted to condemn strongly what it said were ''acts which are against international law'' directed against Libya.   Five members - Venezuela, Ecuador, Nigeria, Gabon and Indonesia -announced that they had to consult their governments before endorsing the condemnation. Ministers said further possible measures against the United States would be discussed Wednesday, but there appeared to be little likelihood they would include oil-related punitive action.   Oil prices on futures markets in London and New York opened higher today on the Libyan news, but fell back in thin trading as investors sold to cash in on the higher price levels.

headline: OPEC STILL DIVIDED ON OIL CURBS
abstract: Ministers of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries muddled through a sixth day of talks today, but remained at odds over proposals for new production ceilings to stop the oil price slide.   Sheik Ahmed Zaki Yamani, Saudi Arabia's oil minister, told reporters at the close of this morning's discussions, ''We are moving, but it's a long, long way still.''   Delegates said three ministers -from Indonesia, Nigeria and Kuwait - were appointed to try to decide what kind of output cuts OPEC can reasonably ask of five non-OPEC countries that have shown a certain willingness to cooperate, after a majority of OPEC ministers tentatively agreed on Saturday to production ceilings for the rest of this year.   Delegates said all the members, except for Algeria, Libya and Iran, had approved a cumulative ceiling averaging 16.7 million barrels a day over the year, which would be achieved by curtailing production to 16.3 million barrels a day in the second and third quarters of 1986 and 17.3 million barrels in the last quarter.

headline: FIVE ARRESTED IN SMUGGLING OF $400 MILLION IN HEROIN
abstract: The owner of a Madison Avenue beauty parlor and four others were arrested by Federal investigators yesterday on charges of smuggling up to $400 million worth of Turkish-grown heroin into the United States by hiding it in the cosmetic bottles of their couriers.   The United States Attorney in Brooklyn, Reena Raggi, said at a press conference that the arrest was the first in four years in the New York area involving Turkish heroin.   She said, however, that the ring was typical of those in a number of recent cases involving ''small, emerging groups'' importing from Nigeria, Southeast Asia and other areas, who have become significant brokers in heroin trafficking as organized-crime groups in the United States have pulled back.   The heroin was smuggled into the country through Kennedy International Airport, Miss Raggi said.

headline: MOST CHILE EXILES STILL KEEPING THEIR DISTANCE
abstract: More than a dozen years since Chileans began to flee their homeland for political reasons, only a few have returned, and critics of the military Government point to the exile issue as one of the worst stains on the national conscience and image.   Many who do not share the largely leftist political views of the exiles express outrage at their continuing banishment, saying that one of the most painful things a person can suffer is not being allowed to come home.   Only about 2,000 people have returned from political exile out of 200,000 who fled, according to Humberto Lagos Schuffeneger, a lawyer at the Vicariate of Solidarity, the human-rights office of the Archdiocese of Santiago. Mr. Lagos, who spent five years in Belgium for what he described as ''some problems,'' said 40,000 to 45,000 of those abroad are considered to be actual exiles and the remainder of the 200,000 are family members. #3,719 Prohibited From Returning Of the exiles, only 3,719 are specifically prohibited from returning, their names having been published on the exclusion lists of the Ministry of Interior. But Mr. Lagos said that others were kept out because they acquired the citizenship of the country where they took asylum and that still others were hindered by bureaucratic red tape. But the majority, he said, do not return because of a combination of economic concerns and ''the fact that the same political conditions exist that provoked exile in the first place.''

headline: PHOTOJOURNALISM THAT COLORS THE NEWS IN MANY WAYS
abstract: Because it reaches millions of people every day, and directly affects their thoughts, photojournalism can be considered one of the liveliest visual achievements of the 20th century. Out of this genre, that records the ''real'' world of small and large events, have come many images now firmly imprinted on our consciousness - among them Robert Capa's photograph of a rifleman stopped in midstride by a bullet during the Spanish Civil War, Dorothea Lange's portraits of Depression-numbed migrants, the starved babies of Biafra as witnessed by Donald McCullin, a street scene involving a small boy and two bottles of wine immortalized by the lens of Henri Cartier-Bresson.   But is photojournalism ''art,'' given our traditional concept of art as privileged to escape the burden of ''facts''? Or is it merely reporting? The question, which goes back to the beginnings of the genre in the 1920's and 30's, has often been argued, though as time goes on the need for the argument seems less and less compelling. Yet here it is, raised again, in a provocative exhibition, ''On the Line: The New Color Photojournalism,'' at the Walker Art Center (through June 1, and then on a countrywide museum tour, which bypasses New York). The show presents a dozen photojournalists, ranging in age from the late 20's to the mid-40's, each exhibiting 10 works. The gamut is from grim scenes of bombing in Lebanon by Yan Morvan and Alfred Yaghobzadeh - advocacy photojournalism to be sure - to a folksy series of small-town baseball vignettes by David Burnett.

headline: SOVIET PROTEST BARS ORWELL PLAY FROM FESTIVAL
abstract: A stage production of George Orwell's ''Animal Farm'' scheduled as part of Theater of Nations, an international festival to be held in Baltimore next month, has been canceled because Soviet officials protested its inclusion in the festival.   The decision to exclude ''Animal Farm'' was made by Wole Soyinka, the prominent Nigerian playwright who has been imprisoned and tortured for his criticism of his own Government's policies. Mr. Soyinka is president of the group sponsoring the festival, the International Theater Institute, a nongovernmental organization originally founded by UNESCO.   ''Animal Farm'' - a National Theater of Great Britain production directed by Sir Peter Hall, who is director of the National - was specifically chosen by the Theater of Nations for the festival. But after meeting with Soviet representatives, who objected to the festival's inclusion of the play, Mr. Soyinka told the National Theater that some of the 62 nations represented in the International Theater Institute might be embarrassed by the production, a stage adaptation of the famous 1945 novel satirizing a totalitarian state.

headline: FESTIVAL'S BAN ON ORWELL GETS MIXED REACTION
abstract: Producers, publishers, actors and others involved in the arts responded with a mixture of anger and resignation at the decision to withdraw a stage production of George Orwell's ''Animal Farm'' from an international theater festival in Baltimore.   The production, a stage adaptation of the 1945 novel satirizing a totalitarian state, was excluded from the Theater of Nations festival after Soviet representatives objected.   While some were sympathetic to the predicament presented to Wole Soyinka, the Nigerian playwright, who is president of the group sponsoring the festival, many others were critical of his decision to exclude ''Animal Farm'' and said it constituted a dangerous precedent for impeding artistic freedom and free speech.   ''We start wandering into an uncharted sea when we respond to requests to withdraw works of political opinion,''said Martin E. Segal, chairman of the board of Lincoln Center.

headline: STORM OVER 'ANIMAL FARM' DISPUTE

headline: COMMONWEALTH DELEGATES CHART DRIVE FOR SOUTH AFRICA SANCTIONS

Botha had pulled back from a clear opportunity for negotiations with black leaders who wanted to make an effort for a peaceful settlement.   They contended that the failure of their mission made sanctions a necessity for Western nations, especially Britain. A Tragedy, Australian Says    The two were midway in their presentation here of the 68-page final report of a Commonwealth mission known as the Eminent Persons Group when they were handed a bulletin reporting the reimposition of a state of emergency in South Africa. headline: EXCERPTS FROM REPORT ON SOUTH AFRICA ISSUED BY COMMONWEALTH MISSION
abstract: Following are excerpts from the report on South Africa issued here today by the Commonwealth mission known as the Eminent Persons Group:   During the preliminary visit, General Obasanjo was permitted to see Mr. Mandela. Thereafter, the full group met with him on two occasions, although not with other detainees.   The group approached the meetings with Mr. Mandela with another measure of care. It was impossible not to be aware of the mythology surrounding him, but equally, we were determined that it should not color our impressions or influence our judgment. As far as possible, we resolved to approach these meetings with an open mind. headline: TRADITIONAL HAND TOWELS OF JAPAN
abstract: Myriad are the uses for tenugui (pronounced tay-nu-gui) the graphically striking cotton hand towels traditionally used in Japan for mopping up spilled tea, tightly twisted as a sweatband (witness the sushi chef) or spread over a repast awaiting guests. Free from the confines of Japanese tradition, the ingenious shopper, inspired by the wealth of stunning designs, can devise any number of other uses - dinner napkins (average size is about 10 by 15 inches, but many are larger), place mats, dresser-top runners, dish or guest towels.   Onoya is one of two or three shops in Tokyo still specializing in tenugui. The proprietor, Suzuki Hikokichi, says that his family took over ownership in 1874 from another house, but he does not know how much earlier they had started the business. The shop originally specialized in tabi, the split-toe socks worn with the thong sandals or clogs that are correct for men and women to wear with a kimono. Onoya still carries tabi in heavy cotton ($6.85 to $11.50) in black or white and a small range of colors. The best quality and more expensive ones are made especially for Onoya. Piecing together two different weights of cloth to make the fully lined socks so that the seams don't split is the tricky part of making good tabi. Cotton velveteen tabi, worn by the Japanese only for casual wear, are also stocked in deep tones of green, blue, maroon and black ($13.75).

headline: OPEC AGAIN FAILS ON OUTPUT QUOTAS
abstract: A meeting of OPEC oil ministers appeared to be unraveling today, snagged on the crucial issue of individual production quotas for member nations.   A majority of the ministers apparently did agree to seek to limit the group's crude oil production to an annual average of 17.6 million barrels of oil a day, from a current actual output of about 18 million barrels, to help lift crude oil prices to a range of $17 to $19 a barrel in the third and fourth quarters of this year.   But a group of at least four countries, including Iran, Libya, Algeria and Gabon, rejected the ceiling and price goals. And the conference president, Rilwanu Lukman, Nigeria's oil minister, canceled a briefing for reporters after it became clear that the ministers had been unable to agree on the quota system.

headline: BRIGHT SIDE FOR MINISTERS

headline:

abstract:
EVEN though East End galleries frequently highlight that area's talent, the current installation at the Vered Art Gallery stands out because it updates recent New York exhibitions for its four participants: Helen Hoie and Miriam Schapiro of East Hampton, and Elizabeth de Cuevas and Howard Kanovitz of Amagansett.

Provocative issues lie beneath the ebullience in Miriam Schapiro's collage-paintings, for her themes deal allegorically and introspectively with the concept of presenting oneself to the world. The idea is developed through performance images - high-stepping, leaping, boldly colored figures - whose playful forms may take us by surprise. They achieve their goal, however, in part because they manage to capture and also hold attention.

headline: Both Sides of Debate Are Stirring Reaction

headline:

abstract:
Developments in the United States frequently hold tremendous significance for other nations; yet all too often, American television carries only sketchy coverage of how events and actions originating here are perceived in foreign countries. ''The Foreign Correspondents,'' a discussion series beginning this Saturday afternoon at 3:30 on the Cable News Network, will try to provide some of those missing viewpoints.

Each weekly half-hour program will bring together journalists from several nations to debate the repercussions of American events on their respective countries. The journalists - most of whom are based in Washington, D.C., or New York - who have agreed to appear in the series include Claude Moisy, of Agence France Presse, the French news agency; Yoshio Murakami, from Japan's daily Asahi Shimbun; Wolf Blitzer of The Jerusalem Post; as well as correspondents for newspapers, magazines and broadcast media in Egypt, Nigeria, West Germany, England, Brazil, Italy and others. headline: ARATA ISOZAKI: FROM JAPAN, A NEW WAVE OF INTERNATIONAL ARCHITECTS
abstract: ON A RECENT AFTERNOON, the Okanoyama Graphic Art Museum in Nishiwaki, Japan, was stage and backdrop for an unusual outdoor fashion show - a show that the building itself, designed by the Tokyo architect Arata Isozaki, managed to steal. A group of five traditional Japanese drummers, wearing kimonos and headbands, called the program to order with fast, warring beats. Then a poky, forgetful one-man band took over in a Ringo Starr way, drumming when he remembered, as fashion models in billowing silk robes by the internationally known designer Issey Miyake sailed between the thick concrete columns of the museum's classical front portico.   The museum, completed in 1984, was less than 100 feet away from railroad tracks, and when an evening train pulled by, it became clear that Isozaki had designed the building for this moment. Side by side, neck and neck, museum and train were a pair - the same width and length, even the same colors. The portico's tightly packed group of eight columns looked like an architectural locomotive at the head of the museum's several rooms, which were shaped and roofed like boxcars. The site itself was a scenario, and the fashion show was complete.

headline: 'The Africans': An Attack On Western Values
abstract: Attention must be paid to ''The Africans.'' The nine-part series makes a statement: The West is responsible for all of Africa's afflictions. The operative word here is ''all.'' Political corruption, moral decay, telephones that do not work in Lagos - it is hard to think of a single African problem the series does not trace to the West. In itself this is not important; television series come and go, and although ''The Africans'' has created a controversy, the controversy will be forgotten by next season. Dismiss ''The Africans'' as a random shot, however, or a piece of television programming gone astray, and you miss the reasons it is significant. ''The Africans'' is laden with academic credentials; it is supposed to be the centerpiece of the public-television season; it is being offered as a course for college credit. In the battlefield of ideas, it occupies a prominent place.

headline: CREATIVE STAGES
abstract: For one night only, Alice Tully Hall at Lincoln Center is a cultural crossroads, or maybe a cloverleaf.   During the course of the evening, some six dozen performers appear on the stage, among them a Brazilian samba troupe, a Puerto Rican bomba band, an American funk band, an African percussion group and a gospel choir. Surrounded by the drummers and singers is a photorealist backdrop - clouds, sky, a section of a sequoia - and, in the center of the stage, a story about the birth and death of a warrior ant is narrated alternately by four New York actors and the Nigerian drummer Babatunde Olatunji, and it is later enacted by several serene Bunraku puppets from Japan.   This performance, in all its polycultural glory, is a workshop for the Prologue and Epilogue of ''The Warrior Ant,'' a musical epic-in-progress by the writer-director Lee Breuer and the composer Bob Telson, who have collaborated on the doo-wop opera ''Sister Suzie Cinema'' and the Greek-tragedy-cum-gospel-concert, ''The Gospel at Colonus.''   Along with the many other composers, librettists, directors and singers working on new forms for the music theater, Breuer and Telson have enthusiastically embraced the idea of unfinished, work-in-progress performances - workshops where pieces do their growing up in public.

headline: Fela Anikulapo Kuti's Afro-Beat
abstract: FELA ANIKULAPO KUTI, the dissident Nigerian songwriter and band leader, gave a triumphant concert Saturday night at the Felt Forum. It was his first New York show since 1970 and the first New York appearance of his band, Egypt 80 - 20 musicians, 4 backup singers and 6 dancers. It was also proof that 18 months in a Nigerian prison, on charges that were later dismissed, had not stopped Mr. Kuti or his music. (Mr. Kuti was arrested Sept. 4, 1984, as he and the band were leaving for an American tour; he was released this April.) As outspoken and defiant as ever -he even performed past the 11 P.M. curfew imposed by union overtime fees - Mr. Kuti gave his music a hard-edged authority. He is a charismatic, eccentric performer, part musician and part public figure; between songs, he casually addressed the audience as ''man'' while underlining the messages in his lyrics. He is also, at the age of 48, a taut, well-muscled, almost feline dancer.

headline: CALLS DEALS VITAL; Secret Dealings Have Made Use Of Complex Net
abstract: The secret movement of American military equipment to Iran over the last 18 months was accomplished through an international network of ships, planes, middlemen and companies, according to American and Israeli officials, participants and Iranian dissidents. The three deliveries, believed to contain millions of dollars worth of military materiel, coincided with the release of American hostages.

headline: Out of Zaire, With Paradox

He also has been working diligently to prepare for Mr. Mobutu's trip to Washington next month.

headline: Chevron's Angola Unit Copes
abstract: In the United States, his boss appears in satirical ''wanted'' posters charged with the crime of ''supplying $2 billion-plus of aid and comfort annually to America's Soviet enemy in Cuban-occupied Angola.''   But this week's headache for Will M. Lewis, the manager of the Chevron Corporation's local subsidiary, is not the divestment campaign run by American conservatives but the hardheaded draft boards run by Angola's Army that keep turning his well-trained oil workers into soldiers.   ''Platform operators, personnel at the terminal and treating plants -we have a lot of time invested in these guys,'' Mr. Lewis said in his 12th-floor office here of the latest roundup of draftees from the Chevron subsidiary, the Cabinda Gulf Oil Company. $1.3 Billion Investment The draft is just one of a variety of challenges facing the American business executive, who manages a $1.3 billion investment in a country that does not have diplomatic relations with the United States and that has suffered from 11 years of white flight and civil war that have caused a steady disintegration of essential services.   The incentive to cope is clear: after Nigeria, Angola is black Africa's second-largest oil producer. headline: IN THE HEART OF AFRICA
abstract: THE ROAD TO Nsukka in eastern Nigeria is rutted and crumpled, the aging asphalt torn like a ragged strip of tar paper.   In the midday heat, diesel trucks hauling cassava and market women to the next town kick up clouds of fine yellow-orange dust that linger in the air. Strings of one-story cement buildings in dull pastels with brooding eaves hug the roadside here and there marking small pinpoints of commerce; hand-lettered signs proclaim the ''Decency Food Canteen,'' ''God's Time Hotel,'' ''Praise the Lord Watch Repairers.'' The road is not unlike many of the back-country thoroughfares that try to weave the villages of this vast continent together with urban lights. But for those who remember the details of one of the most savage wars of the 20th century, this area has a special significance. Almost two decades ago, Biafra's secessionist war erupted near here. Today, memories of the two-and-a-half-year conflict persist: of the atrocities committed by both sides, of the heroism displayed by Biafrans under siege by a vastly superior army, of the two million people who perished, mostly through starvation. Yet much of the bitterness, the hatred that prolonged the war far beyond any hopes of success for Biafra, is gone. In one of Africa's rare examples of conscious ethnic harmony, the Ibo people of eastern Nigeria -who had wanted secession - coexist peaceably with the Yoruba and the Hausa-Fulani and the many other groups populating the rest of Nigeria. In fact, until recently, the second-ranking member of Nigeria's military Government was Commodore Ebitu O. Ukiwe, who had commanded the paltry Biafran Navy during the civil war.

headline:
THE LIVELY ARTS;
HANDS OF AN ARTIST, VOICES OF DRUMS
abstract:
ONE recent Sunday afternoon, as a dozen or so visitors to the Nassau County Museum of Fine Art wandered through the current exhibition of African traditional and modern art, they came upon an impromptu pot drum concert.

Frank Giorgini, the artist who made the drums, and Jamey Haddad, a professional musician, played the 20 or more shiny black ''udu'' pots, the traditional drums of the Ibo tribe of Nigeria.

The crowd was pleased as they played together that day. Now the museum, in Roslyn Harbor, has scheduled a repeat performance for Wednesday at 8 P.M.

It was in 1974 that Mr. Giorgini, a native of Copiague, first came into contact with Ibo pot drums. By that time he had earned bachelor's degrees in industrial design and fine arts from the Pratt Institute in Brooklyn. That summer, while he was at the Haystack Mountain School of Arts and Crafts in Maine, he started working with Abbas Ahuwan, a potter and instructor from Nigeria and an expert in the little-known art of making the musical side-hole pot drum.

headline: OIL PRICES MOVE UP, AT LEAST FOR NOW
abstract: OPEC's agreement to slash output by 7 percent in the first half of 1987 sent oil prices above $17 a barrel for the first time since September. OPEC's target is $18 a barrel, but most analysts say the spurt in prices was an overreaction to the OPEC agreement. Reached after two weeks of disharmonious talks led by Rilwanu Lukman, Nigeria's oil minister and the chairman of OPEC, the agreement requires all members except Iraq to cut production. More significantly, it requires them to adhere to a price system for crude products that analysts say will not likely be followed. Other OPEC agreements have failed as members - fearful of losing revenues - cheated on quotas or undercut pricing agreements.   The effect of any increase on heating oil and gasoline prices remains uncertain, however, because those refined products often do not respond until crude prices stabilize. But most analysts expect at least slight increases at the pump, possibly dampening Americans' new-found enthusiasm for driving.

headline: Appraising African Art Through Western Eyes
abstract: "Closeup: Lessons in the Art of Seeing African Sculpture" is an attempt to deal with the paradox of the Western perception of African art. On the one hand, the visual refinement and sophistication of the European tradition has enabled Western artists to be highly responsive to the inventiveness and dynamism of African art. On the other, this visual orientation has a tendency to blind or distance Westerners from African art's essential and very different reality.   "Just looking at, not touching, feeding, conversing with, or otherwise living with these figures is not very African," the photographer Jerry L. Thompson has written in the catalogue to the show. But he concludes that it is the Western involvement with vision, "our exuberant and subtle refinement of visual skill, that gives us access to African sculpture."   The exhibition argues for the importance of appreciating African sculpture as sculpture - not as artifact, or as implement, or as object that can make sense only within its own context. It is clear from the catalogue that the works in the show can be appreciated from the perspective of Greek sculpture, which demands to be seen in the round; from the perspective of Michelangelo, who felt the magic of materials and the need to release the image imprisoned in the stone; and from the perspectives of the modernist developments partly inspired by African art, including Cubism, with its belief in transformation and shifting points of view.   Not only is it all right to look at African art through Western eyes, the exhibition suggests, but it is through Western eyes that the sculptural imagination of African art can be fully appreciated.   The implications of this point of view are clear. Approaching art solely within its own context is never enough to make the case for the richness and scope of any artist or artistic tradition. Great art can always be approached from many directions. Great art always has some common ground with other great art.   But a visual and sculptural approach to African art has limits, as both the catalogue and the printed material available in each room make clear. African art was not made only to be looked at; often its feet or bases are not level, indicating that works were not intended to stand on display. "Many works were kept in dark places and were seen by few people," Susan Vogel, the executive director of the museum, writes in the catalogue. Many of the wooden figures and masks in this show were meant to be worn, carried or held. A number of the objects were oiled, which was a way of preserving, washing and feeding them. An African sculpture could be worshiped, like an ancestral spirit, or tended, like a flower or a tree. It was, Dr. Vogel writes, a "new being."   The six-year-old Center for African Art, on Manhattan's upper East Side, has approached African art in a variety of ways, including anthropologically, historically and esthetically. The museum takes risks. It does not toe a party line.   The 110 objects in this exhibition come from two first-rate private collections. One belongs to Udo Horstmann, a businessman living in Zug, Switzerland. The other collector, an American, is anonymous. Most of the works date from the 19th and 20th centuries. Not everything is well suited to an exhibition that wants its works to be understood in terms of sculptural issues like volume and space, solid and void, internal energy and scale. A number of objects are simply artifacts, without any particular sculptural distinction.   On one level, the exhibition is a response to the distorting effects of the late-modernist belief that flatness is truer than volume, and two-dimensional art is somehow better than three-dimensional. Dr. Vogel writes that the idea for the show (which continues through March 24) grew out of an observation: "I noticed that people in our galleries rarely looked at the sculptures on display from more than one angle. They looked at three-dimensional objects as if they were looking at paintings, or perhaps reliefs that could be appreciated from a single point."   In general, the sculptural figures in this show are self-contained. They seem indifferent to whether or not they are seen. Whether or not the spaces or voids within them are pronounced, they are important. Through them the composed, self-controlled bodies and heads enter into an active relationship with their environment.   Space may seem to accommodate itself to, even hug, the surface and armature. In the elongated Senufo figure from the Ivory Coast, standing upright, her long arms resting on her squat legs, space seems to have nestled between arms and torso like a bird.   The bulkiest sculpture in the show ("the biggest piece of African sculpture I know," Dr. Vogel said), a seven-foot Urhobo mother and child from Nigeria, seems almost held up by space. The massive female figure, frontal and seated, holding her child like a gun, her legs slightly bent, was a shrine to maternity and procreation. Her collarbone, shoulders and arms are a single sculptural shape that seems to have the capacity to revolve. The small, springy, almost insignificant space circulating in and around the squat, steadfast legs seems to hold up her body and give it the power to react.   Any visitor to this show will encounter 10 or 12 objects that suggest what sculpture can be. A standing, big-bellied, bug-eyed figure from the Donga River region in Cameroon seems to have been not so much carved as squeezed and squashed into frozen shape by the pressure of space.   From the front, a six-inch-high neck rest from Zaire is a seated female figure with one hand on her belly and the other on her ribs. Seen from the back, the arms become a bow, her back an arrow and her hair like ringed, rooflike disks.   A four-inch Luala man from Zaire, seen head on, places his hands pensively on his neck as energy seems to spring from his legs and arms into his head. From the sides, his arms are musical, like a harp, or active, again like a bow. From the back, his hands merge with the neck and his body resembles a natural or architectural vault. He is actively and creatively at rest.   The exhibition calls attention to some of the main characteristics of African sculpture. The figures are usually erect. A vertical column running through them seems indestructible. Most sculptures were carved from a single block of wood. The spinal column of a figure suggests the core of a tree. Not only does the spinal column hold a figure together but sometimes the arms and head seem fed by it, like branches by a trunk. In a standing female figure-stool from Zaire, the column running upward from the buttocks seems to be pumping juice into the breasts and head.   The sense of weight and conviction of this figure-stool is a result of what seems to be tremendous internal pressure. The eyes and mouth of the woman are squeezed tight as her face and breasts project - are almost thrown - forward. The skin of her silent, slow, fecund body seems swollen from the tidal flow of the life inside it.   There is a point, however, at which the exhibition runs into trouble. It resists one prominent current cliche, which is that looking at one culture through the eyes of another is inevitably an act of violence and imperialism. But it comes close to falling into another, which is that art that is intended to be lived with as if it were a living being is automatically more substantial than art that is made to be seen.   Dr. Vogel writes that the African audience for the works in the show "was not seeking the purely visual contact that we in the West associate with looking at art; their experience was fuller and more complex," made up of sound, belief, anticipation and understanding. "Even tastes and aromas might be part of the whole esthetic pleasure as many masquerade festivals were also feasts."   If she is saying that African art is more integrated than modern Western art into the daily life and ritual of its community, that is one thing. If she is saying that the African experience of African art is fuller and more complex than, let's say, the Westerner's experience of Western painting or photography, that is another.   There is no such thing as "purely visual contact." Experiencing painting or photography is no more purely visual, no more intrinsically separated from the rest of experience, than looking at a sunset, or looking into the eyes of a lover or friend, or reading a book you can't put down. The experience of looking at a painting or sculpture may be full enough and complex enough to inspire and resist a lifetime of explanations.   Although none of the objects in this show can be touched, as most of them were intended to be, their impact is clear. This is the kind of exhibition that can initiate people to African art and help those who already care about it to see it better.

headline: Place-Kicker Target of Inquiry
abstract: The way Donald Igwebuike has apparently been telling it, all he did was send some money home to his parents in Nigeria. The way Federal authorities seem to be viewing it, that would have been fine if the friend the Minnesota Viking place-kicker used as a courier hadn't returned to the United States with 31 small bags of heroin in his stomach.   That was a couple of weeks ago, and since the friend's arrest at the Orlando, Fla., airport, Igwebuike, who spent five years with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers before joining the Vikings this fall, has been the target of an investigation by Federal authorities in Tampa, Fla.   The Tampa authorities weren't available for comment last night, but according to a report on ABC's "World News Tonight", they say they have "irrefutable evidence" linking Igwebuike to the drug deal, including his participation in phone conversations indicating that he was aware of the transaction.   Igwebuike was referring all inquiries to his lawyer, who couldn't be reached last night. The Vikings, who learned about the matter from reporters, would say only that they had not been contacted by Federal authorities, that they had talked to Igwebuike and his lawyer and that they had referred the matter to the National Football League.

headline: David G. Scanlon, 69, African-Studies Expert
abstract: David G. Scanlon, a retired professor of international education at Teachers College of Columbia University, died on Thursday at Boston University Hospital. He was 69 years old and lived in Orleans, Mass.   He died of cancer, said a spokesman for the Nicherson Funeral Home.   Dr. Scanlon, who specialized in African studies, directed the Institute for Education in Africa at Teachers College, which trained teachers for the Peace Corps in several African countries, from 1956 to 1970. He traveled extensively in Africa and lived for a time in Uganda. During the long conflict between Nigeria and Biafra, Dr. Scanlon, a Quaker, represented the American Friends Service Committee in relief work.   In 1970 he retired from Teachers College because of an illness. He later joined Cape Cod Community College in Barnstable as professor of history, and established a program in international studies. He retired in 1983.   Dr. Scanlon was born in Leominster, Mass., was a graduate of Fitchburg State Teachers College in Massachusetts and held a doctorate from Teachers College. He served for two years with Unesco, establishing schools in the interior of Liberia.    He wrote several books on African and international education and was co-editor of the World Yearbook of Education from 1968 to 1970.   He is survived by his wife, Mary, and a daughter, Judith, of Kingston, Mass.

headline: Bulgarian A-Plant Reactors Are Shut Down After Mishap
abstract: Technicians at Bulgaria's sole nuclear plant closed down two of its five reactors today because of a breakdown, the official news agency reported.   The brief dispatch said the mishap had occurred outside the plant's nuclear reactor core, but it gave no other details. It said the two reactors, one with a capacity of 440 megawatts and another of 1,000 megawatts, were closed down as a precaution.   The breakdown occurred less than a week after international experts expressed concern about safety at the plant at Kozlodui, on the Danube River in northern Bulgaria. German officials, citing safety problems, have decided to close five reactors of the same Soviet design as the 440-megawatt reactor at Kozlodui.   Prime Minister Andrei Lukanov said on Monday that the plant would be mothballed unless it could meet international safety standards.

headline: LONG ISLAND GUIDE
abstract:
YOUNG MUSICIANS

Over the years, orchestras that showcase talented youngsters have sprung up on Long Island, and this week two of the more-lasting groups will perform.

Today, the Gemini Youth Symphony, which began some 20 years ago as the Training Orchestra, performs in Commack. Under Paul Rudoff's baton, and with Darel Stark, the award-winning young violinist from Port Jefferson, as soloist, the 56-member ensemble will play works by Beethoven, Weber and Bizet. 

The free concert is at 3 P.M. at the Middle School on Vanderbilt Parkway.  On Friday, the Camerata Youth Orchestra, now in its 12th year, opens its new season at a new home, SUNY-Old Westbury. The first of two concerts features the Camerata Chamber Orchestra, conducted by Kenneth Jernigan, in works by Bach and Beethoven at 8 P.M. 

Then at 3 P.M. next Sunday, the Camerata String Orchestra, directed by Roberta Kaufman-Stalzer, will perform pieces by Grieg, Bach and Sowande.

Tickets: 766-5405.
YOUNG AUDIENCES 

 "Classics for Kids (And Grown-ups, Too)" has been a fixture at the Garden City campus of Nassau Community College for 11 years now. The series begins its 12th season today, with the acclaimed Rod Rogers Dance Company performing "Jazz Rhythms and Percussion" at 1:30 and 3:30 P.M. in the College Union Ballroom. 

Future installments include an operatic version of "Rumpelstiltskin," a Tom Chapin concert and a session of tap dancing.

Information: 222-7153.

In Brookville, the Tilles Center's series, "Stage One: The Arts Start Here," is back Saturday with "Time Out of Time." A production of the Mettawee River Theater Company, it uses larger-than-life puppets, masks and music to create unusual theatrics. 

The performances are at 11 A.M. and 2 P.M. at the center, on the C. W. Post Campus of Long Island University. Tickets: 626-3100.
HOLOCAUST PROGRAM 

 To mark the opening of the Holocaust Library, a special section of books and audio and video tapes at the Long Beach Public Library, the Holocaust Memorial Committee of Long Island and the library will hold special dedication activities today.

The observance begins at City Hall at 2 P.M. with speeches, including one by Nechama Tec, a professor of sociology at the University of Connecticut and a Holocaust survivor who has written extensively about her experiences.

Then, after the ribbon-cutting at the adjacent library, there will be a screening of Mat Marmorale's video, "An Overview of Kristallnacht," and a chance to tour "The Courage To Remember," an exhibition circulated by the Simon Wiesenthal Center. 

The panels, composed of photographs, will be on display at the Library, 111 West Park Avenue, through Nov. 15. Hours: 432-7101.
FROM LONDON 
<>

Although she now lives in Merrick, Phyllis Ford is a Londoner, having been born and reared there and musically trained on the British stage and music halls. 

Her background has provided Ms. Ford with a readymade act that she has performed solo in clubs in Europe, New York and Long Island and with a troupe of music hall players called the Pearlies.

Lately, Ms. Ford has taken to the local library circuit, accompanied by a pianist, Danny Hurd. At the Baldwin Public Library at 2:30 P.M. today, she is offering "From Coward to the Beatles: 50 Years of British Popular Music." 

At 3 P.M. next Sunday, in a Veterans Day salute at the Manhasset Public Library, Ms. Ford will perform "Hands Across the Sea," a variation of the same theme. 

Both concerts are free. 
POETS GALORE 

 For some reason -- coincidence, perhaps -- this is a week that all poetry (and prose) lovers can get a healthy fix right from the poets' own lips. 

For example, in a program today that complements its current exhibition, "20th Century Long Island Landscape Painting," the art museum of the Museums at Stony Brook is presenting "Meet Long Island Artists and Poets."

It is a session in which the artists Stan Brodsky, Harvey Dinnerstein and Howard Kanovitz will talk about the impact of the landscape on their work, and the poets David Axelrod, Stanley Barkan and Diana Chang will read their odes to the landscape.

The free program is at 4:30 P.M. and ends with a wine and cheese reception.

On Tuesday, literature fans can sample both the fiction offered by Valerie Martin, whose latest novel, "Mary Reilly," will soon become a Roman Polanski film, and the poetry of Martin Espada, whose roots are in Brooklyn's Hispanic culture, and Maurice Kenny, a Mohawk Indian.

Ms. Martin reads at 12:35 P.M. at Roosevelt Hall on the campus of SUNY-Farmingdale; the poets appear at 7:30 P.M. in the Humanities Building at SUNY-Stony Brook. Both sessions are free.

Finally, on Wednesday there's another doubleheader. Karl Kirchwey, who heads the poetry center at the 92d Street 'Y' in Manhattan, reads at 2 P.M. in the Science Building at Adelphi University's Garden City campus. At 8 P.M., Mr. Kenny who twice has been nominated for a Pulitzer prize, appears again, this time in the Schwartz Library on the C. W. Post Campus of Long Island University in Brookville. 

Both programs are free.
'CUTTING EDGE' FILMS 

 What's a "cutting edge" film? It's an offbeat entry that normally would not make it to the television screen by way of conventional or festival channels. 

But fear not. The International Film Circuit searches the world for what it considers new and exciting films and puts together a package to tour appropriate showcases.  

 On the Island, that showcase is the New Community Cinema in Huntington, which on Wednesday is screening the first of two "cutting edge" double features: Derek Jarman's "The Last of England," billed as "a visionary portrait of the everyday apocalypse," and, from Switzerland, "Macao -- or Beyond the Sea," called "an ironic look at paradise and the power of love."

After Nov. 28, "Dust in the Wind," a film from Taiwan, and "My Favorite Story," a French drama by Anne-Marie Mieville, will be shown. 

Tickets and schedule: 423- 7610. 
'CONNECTION DAY' 

 Everything anyone ever wanted to know about getting the word to the public by way of the media will be on tap Friday, when the Long Island Coalition for Fair Broadcasting holds its annual "Connection Day." 

This is a colloquium featuring seven workshops led by TV, radio and print experts who will give the lowdown about shepherding stories to the media. In other words, "connecting." .

With Tony Guida, a Channel 4 news anchor, as keynoter, and representatives of the major radio, TV, newspaper and magazine outlets covering the Island, participating, "Connection Day" is from 8:30 A.M. to 2:30 P.M. at the Long Island Marriott in Uniondale. 

Reservations: 222-0146.
CHANNEL 21 IS 21 

 One of Long Island's very own media -- Channel 21, the island's first TV station and still its only public TV outlet -- is celebrating its 21st anniversary this year. And it will do it in style with a fund-raising concert by Tony Bennett Friday night at the Westbury Music Fair. 

Mr. Bennett not only will sing for the station -- he will appear in regular performances Saturday and next Sunday at the Music Fair -- but he also has donated one of his pen-and-ink drawings to be auctioned at a champagne reception following the concert.

For reservations for the benefit, which also includes a tribute to Msgr.  Thomas J. Hartman, director of radio and television for the Roman Catholic Diocese of Rockville Centre, call 454-8866.
WILDLIFE FESTIVAL 

 At the Planting Fields Arboretum in Oyster Bay, nature will be celebrated Saturday and next Sunday at the sanctuary's annual Wildlife Festival and Craft Show. 

Devoted to the theme "Wildlife -- Its Gifts and Preservation," the celebrating will be done with live hawks, owls and bobcats, children's storytelling, educational programs and exhibitions and sales of art, crafts and books. 

The festival is from 10 A.M. to 5 P.M. Saturday and 11 A.M. to 4 P.M. next Sunday.

Admission and reservations for "For the Birds," a benefit party Friday at 6 P.M. at the Hay Barn: 922-3200
VOCAL COMPETITION 

 Now in its 30th year, the Long Island Opera Company is taking off in new directions this season. In addition to its regular performing schedule, which includes productions of "La Boheme," "Barber of Seville," and "Il Trovatore," the troupe is holding a vocal competition honoring the company's late artistic director, Bernard Hart.  

 Those vying for the Bernard Hart Memorial Award for Vocal Excellence will sing Saturday at 8 P.M. at the Roslyn Middle School on Powerhouse Road. Tickets-information: 489-0738.

headline: New & Noteworthy
abstract: IN THE NIGHT CAFE, by Joyce Johnson. (Washington Square/Pocket Books, $7.95.) In the early 1960's, as the Beat Generation fades into the counterculture, 26-year-old Joanna Gold falls for a New York City painter who does everything to excess. Last year our reviewer, Phillip Lopate, said this novel "sails on its first-person narration: a fiercely believable, testifying voice that is pungent, close to the bone, stinging with candor."   IN THE NAME OF GOD: The Khomeini Decade, by Robin Wright. (Touchstone/Simon & Schuster, $10.95.) Robin Wright, whose coverage of Iran won a National Magazine Award for The New Yorker in 1989, reveals the method behind the madness of the Khomeini regime. Her book is "the best account of Khomeini's Iran to date, providing a highly readable overview and analysis," Marie Colvin said here last year. " 'In the Name of God' comes as close as is possible to penetrating the obscurity of Teheran."   POODLE SPRINGS, by Raymond Chandler and Robert B. Parker. (Berkley, $4.95.) When Raymond Chandler died in 1959, his estate included the first four chapters of a novel in which Philip Marlowe is married to a rich woman and ensconced in Palm (or, as he calls it, Poodle) Springs, Calif. Three decades later Robert B. Parker, the creator of the private eye Spenser, completed the story. "That Mr. Parker pulls off the stunt is a tribute to his enormous skill," Ed McBain said here last year. "In fact, one of the true delights in 'Poodle Springs' is to watch this engaging writer as first he tests the impossible shackles fastened to his wrists and his ankles, then breaks free of them to charge exultantly down a road Chandler himself might have chosen in his prime."   MY CENTURY: The Odyssey of a Polish Intellectual, by Aleksander Wat. Edited and translated by Richard Lourie. (Norton, $12.95.) No longer able to commit his words to paper, the poet Aleksander Wat spent many of his dying days telling Czeslaw Milosz about his perilous life as a Polish intellectual. The book is "a work of art," Jan T. Gross said here last year. "I would put it on a shelf in the vicinity of Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's 'Gulag,' so compelling is its testimony and analysis."   A STRANGER IN THE KINGDOM, by Howard Frank Mosher. (Laurel/Dell, $9.95.) In a small town in northern Vermont, a black minister is accused of murdering a pregnant 17-year-old girl. Last year our reviewer, Lee Smith, said this book is "both a 'good read' and a fine novel. It is about deeply felt emotion, about prejudice, about the clash between the past and the present, the end of the frontier and of religious differences -- all presented in a lucid, straightforward style that's a pleasure to read."    THE LIFE OF GRAHAM GREENE. Volume One: 1904-1939, by Norman Sherry. (Penguin, $15.95.) Graham Greene's biographer tells how a melancholic boy with a case of wanderlust became a literary giant instead of a burnt-out case. "Norman Sherry's own restless inquiries carefully mirror those of his subject," Robert Coles said here last year, "and show a side of the novelist far more interesting and convincing than the familiar one of the bored or disheartened and troubled upper-class 20th-century existentialist."   HIS THIRD, HER SECOND, by Paul Estaver. (Soho, $9.95.) A twice-divorced 50-year-old with an adopted daughter decides to try his luck with a widow who has three children of her own. "Happy families are a nice switch," Carolyn Banks said here last year. "This is a thoroughly engaging first novel with an enormous range. And what a big-hearted book it is."   THE BROKEN CORD, by Michael Dorris. Foreword by Louise Erdrich. (Harper Perennial, $9.95.) The novelist Michael Dorris tells about the agonies of raising an adopted child doomed to a life of mental cloudiness by a mother who drank during pregnancy. "The alarming statistics and consequences of fetal alcohol syndrome are skillfully interwoven with the human story of one of its victims," Patricia Guthrie said here last year. " 'The Broken Cord' should be required reading for all medical professionals and social workers, and especially for pregnant women, and women who contemplate pregnancy, who may be tempted to drink."   FAILURE TO ZIGZAG, by Jane Vandenburgh. (Avon, $8.95.) Charlotte, the protagonist of this novel, learns about life from a mother who is alcoholic and schizophrenic and works (when she is not institutionalized) as a carnival ventriloquist. "Jane Vandenburgh's depiction of their jagged, tangled lives, though slow moving at first, is superb," Margot Mifflin said here last year.   HOPES AND IMPEDIMENTS: Selected Essays, by Chinua Achebe. (Anchor/Doubleday, $9.95.) In one of these essays, the Nigerian novelist takes on Joseph Conrad and his depiction of Africa as a land of uncivilized darkness. "His thoughts always pack a provocative wallop," Joe Wood said here last year. "Mr. Achebe aims to nudge readers to think past their stubborn preconceptions, and he succeeds marvelously." headline: SAUDI OIL EXPORTS RISE TO NEW HIGH, ERASING SHORTAGE
abstract: Saudi Arabia's oil production surpassed 8.2 million barrels a day this week and is expected to rise to 8.5 million barrels early next year, the highest level in nine years, the Saudi Oil Minister, Hisham Nazer, said in an interview today.
