headline: NOTED WITH PLEASURE
abstract: True Gifts of the Spirit  Modern designers have embraced Shaker theories of clarity and simplicity but ignored the spirit behind Shaker ideas. This is from "By Shaker Hands" by June Sprigg (University Press of New England, paper).   Twentieth-century simplicity is machine-made, out of man-made materials, and the result of a movement in design; the Shaker kind of simplicity was made by hand, of wood or wool or stone by Shaker craftsmen, and the result of a religious movement to create a simple and perfect way of life. Twentieth-century simplicity is more often than not the manufacturer's demand since it means a faster rate of production. But to the Shaker who took all the time he needed to make his work perfect, simplicity was a gift of the spirit. . . .   Nineteenth-century Shakers would probably feel a sharp sense of irony in the fact that we admire them for the things that mattered the least to them, their material goods. We imitate their chairs, while ignoring their charity; we reproduce their tables and oval boxes, and reject their celibacy. How much more the Shaker valued the simplicity and humility of his spirit than the chair he used or the box he made. Thriving on Gossip    Gossip is our communal voice, Hugh Kenner writes -- necessary but of dubious value when used by biographers to re-create a life. This is from "Historical Fictions," a collection of essays and reviews (North Point).   When people give interviews they're telling stories. . . . If we could hear their voices we'd be hearing that very essential human phenomenon, gossip: the endless talk by which people assimilate one another's oddness. Gossip is oral, gossip is an unbounded sphere of speech, renewed without cease. It is never idle, also never objective; it unites those present in a sustaining fiction about someone absent. It thrives in villages, it thrives in all small communities, academic, cultural, professional, it thrives in neighborhoods, thrives wherever people subsist on each other's company, make do with each other's mysteries. . . . Contrariwise, print is a praying mantis, gossip the mate she eviscerates. From gossip the book-writer sucks a goo called information, to cement edifices of assertion with. The Invisible Artist    To understand African art, Chinua Achebe argues (using his own tribe in Nigeria as an example), one must grasp that its most important feature is not the the artist but rather art's function in society. This is from "Hopes and Impediments: Selected Essays" (Anchor/Doubleday, paper).    Part of my artistic and intellectual inheritance is derived from a cultural tradition in which it was possible for artists to create objects of art which were solid enough and yet make no attempt to claim, and sometimes even go to great lengths to deny, personal ownership of what they have created. . . .    Mbari    is an artistic "spectacular" demanded of the community by one or other of its primary divinities, usually the Earth goddess. To execute this "command performance" the community is represented by a small group of its members selected and secluded for months or even years for the sole purpose of erecting a befitting "home of images" filled to overflowing with sculptures and paintings in homage to the presiding god or goddess. These representatives . . . chosen to re-enact, as it were, the miracle of creation in its extravagant profusion, are always careful to disclaim all credit for making, which rightly belongs to gods; or even for initiating homage for what is made, which is the prerogative of the community. Remembrance of Meals Past    One feature all great chefs and gourmets have in common is their ability to recollect and reproduce the savory specifics of a dish. This is from James Beard's "Delights and Prejudices" (Collier/Macmillan, paper).   The ability to recall a taste sensation, which I think of as "taste memory," is a God-given talent, akin to perfect pitch, which makes your life richer if you possess it. If you aren't born with it, you can never seem to acquire it. Great wine palates must depend on taste memory for the sureness of their judgment. . . . Cheese tasters, tea tasters, cognac tasters -- all must depend for a living on the keenness of their taste memories. Great gastronomes also have a highly developed sense memory, or they would not make such a ceremony of tasting and enjoying food. And naturally good chefs and cooks must depend upon memory when they season or when they are combining subtle flavors to create a new sauce or a new dish. The Gaze of Recognition    Jane Goodall's work with chimpanzees raises a question implicit in the study of animal behavior: Can we ever really understand how animals see the world? This is from "Through a Window: My Thirty Years With the Chimpanzees of Gombe" (Houghton Mifflin).   Often I have gazed into a chimpanzee's eyes and wondered what was going on behind them. I used to look into Flo's, she so old, so wise. What did she remember of her young days? David Greybeard had the most beautiful eyes of them all, large and lustrous, set wide apart. They somehow expressed his whole personality, his serene self-assurance, his inherent dignity -- and, from time to time, his utter determination to get his way. For a long time I never liked to look a chimpanzee straight in the eye -- I assumed that, as is the case with most primates, this would be interpreted as a threat or at least as a breach of good manners. Not so. As long as one looks with gentleness, without arrogance, a chimpanzee will understand, and may even return the look. And then -- or such is my fantasy -- it is as though the eyes are windows into the mind. Only the glass is opaque so that the mystery can never be fully revealed.

headline: HOME ENTERTAINMENT/RECORDINGS: RECENT RELEASES
abstract: CLASSICAL Shankar and Glass: 'Passages'  Ravi Shankar and Philip Glass. Private Music 2074-2-P; CD only.      The relationship of Ravi Shankar and Philip Glass goes back a quarter of a century, when Mr. Glass was hired by the Indian musician to transcribe some of his sitar music into Western notation. That encounter opened Mr. Glass to new ways of thinking about rhythm, and the rest is, of course, history. Now, in a recording in which the two pay tribute to one another, Mr. Glass deconstructs Mr. Shankar's elaborate melodies in compositions he recorded with a chamber ensemble in New York, while Mr. Shankar builds intricate sound castles in works he recorded in Madras for himself, orchestra and choir. Mr. Glass and Mr. Shankar always sound themselves, but the pieces do demonstrate just what versatile, boundary-bursting musicians they are.    -- Mark Swed    Bartok: 'Contrasts'; Stravinsky: 'L'Histoire du soldat' Suite; Ives: 'Largo'; Songs (arranged for clarinet)  Richard Stoltzman, clarinet; Lucy Chapman Stoltzman, violin; Richard Goode, piano. RCA Victor Red Seal 60170-2-RC. CD and cassette.    Bartok's "Contrasts," derived from folk dances, was initially to be titled "Rhapsody"; the final version received its Carnegie Hall premiere at the hands of Benny Goodman, Joseph Szigeti and Bartok himself. Such rich blood, high spirits and dazzling craft are the stuff wrought by the present threesome in this heady performance. If Mr. Stoltzman's agile clarinet rules "Contrasts," it is Lucy Chapman Stoltzman's droll violin that puts the scintillating finish on Stravinsky's own arrangement of music from "L'Histoire du Soldat." The arrangements for nine Ives songs add little, and the printed lyrics serve only as a reminder of the peculiar charm that is missing without the singing.   -- Lawrence B. Johnson  Mendelssohn: Third Symphony ('Scottish') and Fourth Symphony ('Italian')  London Classical Players conducted by Roger Norrington (EMI/Angel; CDC 7 54000; CD and cassette); Berlin Philharmonic conducted by James Levine; Deutsche Grammophon 427 670; CD only).     As Mendelssohn conductors, Roger Norrington and James Levine have little in common except that neither is noted for doing Mendelssohn. Not surprisingly, the distance between their versions is wide. Mr. Norrington emphasizes the lean, sometimes pungent or explosive timbres of his early-instrument band. The move into the middle-Romantic repertory is a recent one for them, however, and in many ways the performances sound like sketches, with expressive details to be filled in later. If not for the sonorities and an occasional trick with rhythm or tempo, in fact, a listener could mistake these for performances by a well-drilled but not terribly imaginative modern orchestra. Mr. Levine's readings are traditional in the 20th-century -- but also the best -- sense of the term. The sound is blended and mellow, the lines long and flowing, the pacing broad. Mood as well as texture counts.  -- Andrew L. Pincus Rutter: Te Deum and other church music  Cambridge Singers, City of London Sinfonia, conducted by John Rutter. Collegium Records COLCD 112; CD and cassette.      You might dismiss these amiable compositions as sacred "easy listening." But Mr. Rutter approaches church music the way Rossini and Verdi did, using the vocabulary of contemporary secular music. His melodies and rhythms are not operatic so much as derived from Broadway, film and folk music, and are as appropriate to liturgy as the music of any age. His choral writing is fluent, idiomatic and always expressive of the text. His instrumentation is colorful, his harmony firmly diatonic with occasional hints of commercial glitz. -- Barrymore L. Scherer 'Mitropoulos Conducts Richard Strauss'  Various orchestras conducted by Dimitri Mitropoulos. Hunt Productions 2 HUNTCD 581 (two-disk set) and HUNTCD 583; CD only.      Mitropoulos may be due for a rediscovery, but it is hard to imagine this assortment of eight concert performances from the 1950's igniting the flame. The sound ranges from fair to poor, and the performances -- all charged with a restless intensity -- are even more variable. The best is a heavyweight but vital "Burleske" with the pianist Rudolf Serkin and the New York Philharmonic. A "Symphonia domestica" with the Philharmonic verges on incoherence (an "Alpensinfonie" with the Vienna Philharmonic is not much better), but an alternate "domestica" with the Cologne radio orchestra stands up well. The liner notes mix the inaccurate with the incomprehensible. A once-important recording figure deserves better.-- A. L. P.  POP/JAZZ  Pylon: 'Chain'  Sky 72020-2; all three formats.     Six years afer disbanding, Pylon has returned without missing one of its hard, sharp beats. Along with the B-52's, the band briefly made Athens, Ga., the headquarters for dance-rock in the early 80's; they also showed the far more famous R.E.M. how to make a seductive sound triumph over art-student lyrics. Pylon, whose members learned to play instruments together, still works as a dynamic commune: Curtis Crowe delivers imperious drum jolts; the bassist Michael Lachowski and the guitarist Randy Bewley exchange low, buzzing lead figures, while Vanessa Briscoe Hay mixes soul growls with train-whistle yelps. On "Go" and "Outside" especially, they throw in melodies of ideal, austere sensuality. -- Milo Miles L.L. Cool J.: 'Mama Said Knock You Out'  Def Jam/Columbia 46888; all three formats.     On the rebound from a dud album, "Walking With a Panther," L.L. Cool J. has gone back to street level. He reclaims his persona as the most articulate of homeboys, above uncluttered funk riffs assembled by the producer Marley Marl. L.L. Cool J. is back to putting down rivals and praising such simple pleasures as driving a car with a "boomin' system," showing off his boundless gift for analogy and wordplay: "Milky Cereal" works breakfast brand-names into lascivious double-entendres. Balancing the boasts is "Cheesy Rat Blues," a wheezy complaint by a has-been rapper whose friends disappeared with his popularity, and "Illegal Search," about how a young black man's trappings of success draw police harassment. As L.L. Cool J. peeks behind the crass materialism his persona once took for granted, he sounds tougher and funnier.-- Jon Pareles    King's X: 'Faith Hope Love by King's X'  Megaforce/Atlantic 7 82145; all three formats.     Progressive rock, a tired relic of the post-psychedelic era, has rarely sounded as vibrant as it does on the hard-rock trio's third album. Their collision of knotty melodicism, complex vocals and epic lyrical gestures echoes the alchemical affectations of Genesis and Yes. But Ty Tabor's serrated riffing is closer to Metallica in snarl and spirit, while the band's bracing power-pop harmonies recall vintage Badfinger. With the singer-bassist Doug Pinnick wailing atop the mix with gritty, Bono-esque nobility, King's X rams its utopian message home with ferocity and finesse. -- David Fricke Sir Shina Peters: 'Ace'  CBS 1002; LP only (from Stern's Music, 598 Broadway, New York, N.Y. 10012).     African pop music, clearly formulaic, occasionally allows for a bit of change. Enter Sir Shina Peters, Nigeria's newest and most exciting band leader. Mr. Peters -- "the creator of the Afro-juju sound," according to the album's liner notes -- mixes American funk and hip-hop rhythms with the wavelike surge of talking drums. Choruses sing paeans to Mr. Peters, and Mr. Peters sings his own praises. The band, 20 or so strong, rocks; guitars burst into the mix, and song segues into song for album-length pieces in classic, intense juju style. Though it reproduces about a tenth of the wildness of Mr. Peters's live shows, the album is a good example of the endless cross-pollination between worlds.   -- Peter Watrous   Loren Schoenberg and His Jazz Orchestra: 'Just a-Settin' and a-Rockin' '  MusicMasters 5039-2-C; CD only.     The tenor saxophonist combines a scholar's fascination for the offbeat with an improviser's delight in risk-taking. All four of Mr. Schoenberg's big-band swing albums (like those of the American Jazz Orchestra, for which he also serves as orchestra manager) swingingly exalt the fundamentals of jazz repertory: Mr. Schoenberg and his sidemen ad-lib stunningly individual solos in traditional styles, with the most rewarding numbers coming from the mammoth legacies of Duke Ellington and Benny Goodman. Showcasing such superb soloists as the clarinetist Ken Peplowski, the singer Barbara Lea and the late drum giant Mel Lewis, "Just a-Settin' and a-Rockin' " serves up history you can put your foot to.   -- Will Friedwald

headline: Nigeria Is Spared the Worst of AIDS, but Experts Wonder for How Long
abstract: After a long delay that may have lulled Nigerians into a false sense of security, AIDS has begun to creep into the population, especially among prostitutes, prompting warnings that the disease may soon reach the epidemic levels reported elsewhere in sub-Saharan Africa.    The number of cases officially reported so far in Nigeria is small: Out of a population of about 120 million, only 68 people had been diagnosed as suffering from AIDS through the end of September, according to figures from Nigeria's Health Ministry. While the data are far from complete and almost certainly represent an undercount, several independent studies have similarly found a remarkably low rate of the disease.

headline: Bulgaria's Former Leader to Face Charges
abstract: The former Communist leader, Todor Zhivkov, will face trial on charges of misappropriation of funds and abuse of power, Bulgaria's prosecutor general announced today.    The 78-year-old Zhivkov ruled Bulgaria for 35 years but has been under house arrest since he was ousted last year by former colleagues.   Prosecutor General Martin Gounev was quoted by BTA, the official press agency, as saying that Mr. Zhivkov would be tried for misappropriation of $3.7 million. Mr. Gounev gave no date for the trial, but said it would be held soon.   Mr. Zhivkov's right-hand man, Milko Balev, is also to face trial for the misappropriation of funds, BTA reported.   Mr. Zhivkov has admitted he made mistakes but has denied committing crimes.   The announcement came as public pressure mounted on the government of Andrei Lukanov to resign. Mr. Lukanov's Socialist Party, successor to Mr. Zhivkov's Communist Party, won a majority in the June elections and holds 210 of the 400 seats in Parliament.   But Mr. Lukanov has been unable to push his economic reform program, which includes steep price increases, through Parliament. The legislature is to vote on the controversial package on Thursday. Mr. Lukanov has said he would resign if it is not enacted.    The opposition Union of Democratic Forces issued a statement today supporting a call by the trade union confederation Podkrepa for a general strike next week if Mr. Lukanov's Government does not resign before then.

headline: NEW JERSEY GUIDE
abstract:
'AFRICA OYE!'

 A company of 50 tribal dancers and musicians from several countries in Africa will bring "Africa Oye!" to the stage of the State Theater in New Brunswick on Friday.

The show's title means "Long Live Africa!" and the show consists of a history of the customs and cultures of Zaire, Mali, Niger and Guinea brought together on the stage in exotic dances, distinctive costumes, unusual musical instruments and colorful face paint.

The show will open with the Batwa-Ekonda Pygmy tribe dancing a ceremonial tribute to their ancestors. The Pende ensemble of dancers and musicians will follow, wearing spectacular masks and intricate costumes made of straw and palm leaf fibers.

The concert will continue with the Kanouri, a quartet of griots (poetic historian-musicians) who perform on a wind instrument that is centuries old and used in both ceremonial music and to transmit coded messages over long distances.

Also among the performers are the Peul Acrobats, the Babunda from Central Western Zaire, the Percussionists of Guinea, the Mbulie-Hemba dance group and Kandia Kouyate, a musical storyteller. 

The show will be at 8 P.M. at the theater, 19 Livingston Avenue. Tickets are $12, $16, $18 and $22. Information: (201) 246-7469.
BRAHMS CONCERT 

 The Pro Arte Chorale of Paramus and the Sacred Heart Cathedral Symphony Orchestra from Newark will mesh their talents in a concert on Saturday at the John Harms Center for the Arts in Englewood. Carmen Pelton, soprano, and William Sharp, baritone, will be the featured soloists with the 150-voice chorale in the performance of the "German Requiem" by Johannes Brahms.

Ms. Pelton sang the lead in the Pro Arte performance of Gluck's "Telemacco" at John Harms and at Lincoln Center last year. Mr. Sharp is a winner of the Carnegie Hall International American Music Competition as well as other awards and has performed with many major orchestras and opera companies and in music festivals in the United States and abroad.

Bart Folse, music director of Pro Arte, will conduct the concert at 8 P.M. in the center, 30 North Van Brunt Street. Tickets are $15 and $18, or $13 and $16 for students and the elderly, respectively. Information: (201) 445-9052.
'HAVANA SINGS!' 

 "Havana Sings!" -- an anthology of Cuban music from the 19th century to the 1950's -- will be performed by Repertorio Espanol of New York City on Thursday in Mahwah.

European melody is combined with pulsating Afro-Cuban beats in the music of Havana. Selections will include "Martha," "Yours" and "The Peanut Vendor."

Repertorio Espanol presents more than 250 performances of plays, musical and dance events in New York's theaters each year and tours nationally, in Latin America and in Spain. An Obie award winner, the company was founded in 1968. Pablo Zinger is the musical director.

"Havana Sings!" will be presented at 7 P.M. in the auditorium of Ramapo College, 505 Ramapo Valley Road. Tickets are $7, or $5 for students.  Information: (201) 529-7448.
DANCE BENEFIT 

 A dance and buffet will be sponsored by Singles Active for the Environment this evening at the Park Cafe in Paramus to benefit three northern New Jersey environmental groups.

Contemporary music, Broadway tunes and songs from the 1940's and 50's will be among the varied musical styles featured by the cafe's disk jockey.

Save Hackensack River Watershed Action Network, Pollution Crises Now and Citizens for Clean Air will be the beneficiaries of the event. Representatives of each group will briefly discuss the problems they tackle in a forum moderated by Kathy Leddy of S.A.F.E.

The dance-buffet will begin at 7:30 P.M. at the cafe, 1 Mack Drive. Tickets are $25. George DeLuca, owner of the cafe, has donated the buffet, so all proceeds will be contributed to the environmental groups.

Information: (201) 501-0677.
BLACK JOURNALIST 

 Ida B. Wells, a crusading black journalist who led an anti-lynching campaign in Memphis in the late 1800's, will be the subject of a lecture by Paula J. Giddings tomorrow evening at Montclair State College. 

Ms. Giddings, a professor of women's studies at Rutgers University, is the author of "When and Where I Enter: The Impact of Black Women on Race and Sex in America," which included portions on the life of Wells.

As the co-owner of Free Speech, a black newspaper in Memphis, Wells combated increasing violence against blacks by publishing the advice of a friend, William Moss, who was a victim of lynching. He had suggested that blacks "save our money and leave a town which will neither protect our lives and property, nor give us a fair trial in the courts, but takes us out and murders us in cold blood." 

A mass exodus resulted, crippling white businesses and, many observers have said, starting the modern civil rights movement.

Wells also advocated armed self-protection. "A Winchester rifle should have a place of honor in every home," she wrote. "When the white man knows he runs as great a risk of biting the dust every time his Afro-American victim does, he will have a greater respect for Afro-American life."

Ms. Giddings, a graduate of Howard University, has broad experience as an editor and journalist with several major publications and is a contributing editor to Essence magazine. Her latest book is "In Search of Sisterhood: Delta Sigma Theta and the Impact of the Black Sorority Movement." 

The lecture, at 7:30 P.M. in Memorial Auditorium, will be followed by a book signing. The campus is off Valley Road in Upper Montclair, and admission to the lecture is free. Information: (201) 893-7416.

headline: The World: Euphoria Is Just a Memory; The Lands Where Communism Retreated Face a Harsh Season of Adjustment and Doubt
abstract: A YEAR after the collapse of Communism in Eastern Europe, its people -- and those of the Soviet Union -- are entering a winter of deep uncertainty. In Moscow, there is little if any material benefit to show for a half decade of structural change, and the absence is testing the people's confidence in their leadership. In the nations newly free from the Soviet orbit, the euphoria has ended as people and their governments grapple with the difficulties of building a future for themselves. It is a winter of uncomfortable, sometimes traumatic, transition, as New York Times correspondents in the region report in the following survey.  POLAND  Joblessness and Soaring Prices     As the first year of Poland's economic reform program nears its conclusion, the stores remain full of food and other goods, but the prices are beyond the reach of many working-class Poles. Unemployment has risen to 5.5 percent, or one million workers, and many others fear they are about to lose their jobs. Whoever wins the Dec. 9 presidential election will confront a divided Parliament that itself will face re-election in the spring. Meanwhile, officials are increasingly worried about the prospect that Soviet refugees could swarm across the border in search of food.    Poland's ambitious program to speed the transition to capitalism enjoyed widespread support of the public in its early phases, but the first round of presidential voting last week showed there is now substantial disquiet in the land. Stanislaw Tyminski, a political unknown, illustrated the depth of opposition among workers and younger voters when he came in second to Lech Walesa, the Solidarity chairman, in a showing that eliminated the Prime Minister, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, from the competition and prompted him to resign. Although Mr. Walesa failed to achieve a majority in the three-way race, he held a wide lead in the first public opinion poll taken after the election -- 58 percent to Mr. Tyminski's 30 percent. Still, many political observers wondered how any president could push ahead with plans to privatize industry, slash subsidies and close inefficient factories and mines. Mr. Walesa has endorsed the economic plan but has said he would change it in ways he has not spelled out. GERMANY  Promises and Impatience     In what used to be Communist East Germany, many people expected reunification to quickly bring them the bounty of a market economy, particularly after western German politicians promised a quick and painless transition. Now their patience is running out as problems mount. Last week, work stoppages crippled eastern Germany's rail system, and they may have been just a foretaste. While the supply of goods is ample, the level of personal debt among eastern Germans suddenly able to buy Western goods is climbing dangerously; the Government's plans to slash price supports on Jan. 1, a move expected to drive up the cost of nearly everything from rents to manufactured goods, generates the kind of fears that sparked the rail strike. Women, who joined the labor force in large numbers under the Communists and gained considerable economic independence, have been hit particularly hard; their jobs have been cut, and so have family care services that the Government used to pay for.   Despite the economic tensions, most Germans from the east continue to regard Chancellor Helmut Kohl as the sole guarantor of eventual prosperity -- one more reason that there appeared to be little doubt that he and his Christian Democrats would be re-elected in the all-German parliamentary elections today. In the weeks leading up to the voting, the Government tried to keep new pressures on the economy to a minimum -- giving in, for example, when workers at the big Trabant factory in Zwickau threatened to strike if the Government didn't provide the subsidies to maintain production of their funny little cars. Another troubling problem has been street violence among youths in the first weeks after unification. Much of the violence takes on neo-Nazi colorings, with screams of "Heil Hitler" and other Nazi slogans, but youth workers say much of the violence is less a coherent ideology than a cry for attention from a young generation that has lost its bearings in a society free of the strictures of Communist dictatorship. CZECHOSLOVAKIA  Still the Old Shoddiness    A year after Czechoslovakia's gentle revolution, its stores are still well stocked by Eastern European standards -- as they were even during the days of subservience to Moscow -- but the shoddiness of the goods displayed remains, along with the habits of poor service. The Government has announced a privatization plan that takes effect Jan. 1, and there is hope that this will break the bureaucracy's lockgrip on the economy. But it also arouses fears that rents will go up along with prices for nearly all consumer goods. Already, Government efforts to give the Czechoslovak crown, the unit of currency, partial convertibility have caused prices for some goods to rise drastically. The price of the Skoda Favorit, a popular, sturdy automobile, jumped in recent months to about 115,000 crowns, from 65,000, in a country where the average monthly wage hovers at about 3,500 crowns. The gulf crisis and sluggish Soviet oil deliveries have contributed to a doubling of gasoline prices.   For now, the friction between the country's 10 million Czechs and 5 million Slovaks appears to be subsiding. In last week's local elections, nationalist parties did remarkably poorly. Nevertheless, the economic burdens appear to be increasing a susceptibility to all kinds of conspiracy theories and quick solutions. Students who were prominent in the demonstrations that toppled the Communists last year have publicly complained about the slowness of change, while other leaders have complained about the apathy of most students. Scattered demonstrations have protested the lingering Communists in the bureaucracy, and voices call for President Vaclav Havel to get rid of the Prime Minister, Marian Calfa, a former Communist.  ROMANIA  Misery Prevails     Trying to inch its way out of a seemingly permanent state of crisis, the Romanian Government on Nov. 1 ushered in the winter season with the first jolt of economic reform. Prices on some goods jumped as much as 300 percent, but so far the changes have done little to alleviate the shortages that make life a misery for most Romanian consumers. In Bucharest, people still wait for hours in line to get meat, gasoline and other basics; water is periodically shut off, and now as an added insult, cigarettes are suddenly hard to find. Political discontent, which has been brewing all year, has taken on new life with the formation of a new opposition group, the Civic Alliance, and many expect it to crescendo around the turn of the year as the country marks the first anniversary of the overthrow of the Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu. "The only solution, a second revolution," was one chant at an anti-government demonstration on Nov. 21, an appeal expected to feed on the grim living conditions.   Hungary Full Shelves, Now   As winter sets in, Hungarians continue to enjoy a level of prosperity that their neighbors to the east can only dream of. The stores are full not only of Hungarian products, but also of Western goods, and outdoor stands still offer a colorful array of fresh fruits and vegetables that would trigger huge lines in Bucharest, Sofia or Moscow. But for all the outward abundance, Hungarians are also bracing for the shock of 1991. The double-barrel impact of higher oil prices and decreased tax revenues comes on top of an inflation rate that has reached 30 percent and is already forcing some painful choices, for people and their government. Even those who are doing well in Hungary's struggling private sector share the gloomy mood that permeates Budapest today, as their families begin to economize on meat, Sunday outings and purchases that had come to be accepted as part of the Hungarian way of life. Last month's three-day taxi strike, set off by a sudden rise in gasoline prices, made the Government realize the limits of the Hungarian public's patience, and the depths of its frustration with a dropping standard of living. BULGARIA  Signs of Distrust     The first victim of the winter's discontent in Bulgaria was the Government, which last week resigned after three days of strikes and a monthslong campaign by the opposition. The outgoing Prime Minister, Andrei Lukanov, a former Communist who like the rest of his party's leadership became a socialist before winning last June's elections, had tried to form a coalition government to bring the country out of a deepening economic crisis. But his efforts were rebuffed, a sign of the distrust that has produced a virtual paralysis in government and society. Given its historic bonds with the Soviet Union, Bulgaria is suffering the effects of its giant neighbor's decline most keenly. Higher oil prices and lost trade and revenues have pushed the economy to the brink: Bulgaria last spring stopped payment on its $10.5 billion debt. In Sofia, Western diplomats speak darkly of a winter where cutbacks in electricity, shortages of medicine and an inadequate diet could cost lives. YUGOSLAVIA  Seeking Survival     Nothing less than the survival of Yugoslavia itself is at stake this winter, as the federal Government struggles to come up with a formula that will hold together the country's bitterly divided national groups. Serbia, the largest of the six republics, will hold its first parliamentary elections this month, but an expected boycott by ethnic Albanians living in the troubled province of Kosovo will only highlight democracy's difficulties in this Balkan nation. Political uncertainties and ethnic hatreds have clouded attempts at economic reform, led by the federal Prime Minister, Ante Markovic. Even in Slovenia, the northernmost republic, which has historically been the most prosperous, production has dropped, the trade deficit is growing and local governments are running short of cash. SOVIET UNION  The Weariness of Waiting for Results     FOR the second consecutive year, the Soviet Union is entering winter in a mood of deep pessimism. Changes here started earlier than in Eastern Europe but are likely to take longer. With no experience of democracy, most Soviet citizens had unrealistic expectations and now are disproportionately disenchanted.   Last winter, a half-decade into perestroika, anxiety about the availability of food already bordered on panic; again this year food is the first preoccupation of the public. For the average citizen more time than ever goes into the hunt for affordable goods; meanwhile, politicians here and abroad are feeding the anxiety with talk of "famine." The problem is distribution rather than production, and there is no evidence of impending starvation. But in the urban centers, where the disappearance of state-supplied foodstuffs is most dramatic, that is not much consolation.   The level of discontent has made it difficult to enact unpopular measures aimed at moving toward free markets, and outsiders sympathetic to the reform process have begun to worry that hard-liners could seize on the disaffection to destabilize the Government. That fear -- as much as humanitarian concern -- has motivated Germany, for example, to move to send food aid.   The breakdown in food distribution is also a symptom of a breakdown in political power. The union is disintegrating into republics, autonomous regions, provinces, insurgent city councils and even neighborhoods proclaiming sovereignty. President Mikhail S.  Gorbachev has power -- the military, K.G.B., the police -- without authority. His rival, Boris N. Yeltsin, President of the Russian republic, has authority -- the ability to direct popular behavior -- without a real grip on power. The political drama of the season is the effort to find some kind of a coalition that will unite power and authority, and stabilize the union. But at the moment the two men are in head-on competition.   Mr. Gorbachev's proposal for a new treaty defining the federal union seems to be a dead letter. Five or six republics have declared flatly that they will not sign it, and Russia will not go along unless it is assured real sovereignty, meaning the superiority of its laws over Soviet law -- something Mr. Gorbachev cannot accept. But Mr. Gorbachev is holding firm to his course, hoping the tide will shift as the public grows frustrated with the lingering political paralysis. Mr. Yeltsin, meanwhile, is trying with some success to set up a kind of Soviet commonwealth; bilateral treaties with other republics seem to hold more promise for the union than Mr. Gorbachev's proposals.    The public is basically furious at everyone. People have lost much of their faith in the ability of democratic politics to get them out of the mess, and a strong yearning for "decisive measures" -- although not, apparently, for dictatorship -- extends to economic as well as political measures.    Mr. Gorbachev is increasingly held personally culpable, and he seems incapable of winning back the public's trust. Mr. Yeltsin remains hugely popular, but lesser democrats are already beginning to lose their luster as the public tires of windy televised debates and sees nothing in the stores; Mr. Yeltsin, too, could face such a decline.

headline: Chad President Reportedly Flees and Rebels March In
abstract: President Hissen Habre and his Cabinet fled the country today after a series of rebel victories, and guerrillas marched later into the capital, Western diplomats said.   The diplomats said Mr. Habre and members of his Government sought refuge in neighboring Cameroon.   As the rebels closed in on Ndjamena, soldiers threw away their guns and uniforms, leaving the city practically undefended. Civilians and renegades from the Chadian Army were looting the capital.   France began organizing the evacuation of its citizens and other foreigners living in this north-central African nation, a former French colony. In Washington, a State Department spokeswoman said that Americans would be boarding French-chartered and commercial planes in the capital on Sunday and Monday.  Rebel Advance Patrols     It was not immediately known how many rebels marched into the city, but it appeared that the guerrillas were mainly advance patrols. Most of the rebels appeared to have remained in eastern Chad, where they have made significant incursions.   The rebels' biggest victory had been the capture on Thursday of Abeche, an eastern town of about 30,000 people 500 miles from Ndjamena.   The rebels, led by a former chief of the armed forces, Idris Deby, are armed by Libya, the diplomats said. But there was no indication that Libya was involved in the latest fighting.   Libya, which has made historical claims to parts of Chad, denies involvement in the rebel offensive, which began Nov. 10.   Mr. Deby helped Mr. Habre, 48 years old, oust former President Goukouni Oueddei from power in 1982. Troops Urged to Disarm     Agence France-Presse quoted people in Ndjamena as saying that Mr. Deby would march into the capital on Sunday at the head of an army of guerrillas and Government deserters.   Alingue Bawayeu, president of Chad's National Assembly and apparently the highest-ranking Government official left in Ndjamena, appealed for calm in an address on Chad radio. He said negotiations were under way with Mr. Deby.   Mr. Bawayeu, who is under the protection of French troops, said he was leading an interim government comprised of National Assembly members and urged soldiers to lay down their weapons.   Western diplomats in Ndjamena and high-ranking officials in Paris, all speaking on the condition that they not be identified, said Mr. Habre and his family fled to neighboring Cameroon in a military transport plane before dawn today. Cars Seized by Soldiers     They said Government Ministers and their entourages escaped across a bridge into Cameroon, just west across the Chari River from Ndjamena.   Some officials remaining in the capital said Mr. Habre had left Ndjamena to direct attacks against rebel forces.   Troops deserted after rumors spread of Mr. Habre's flight. Angry citizens attacked Government buildings or fled to Cameroon. Military boots and uniforms littered the roadsides, apparently left behind by deserters hoping to avoid reprisals from the rebels.   Many soldiers turned their rifles on motorists and commandeered cars for the trip to Cameroon or Nigeria, which lies further west across the northern tip of Cameroon. Others threw away their weapons, which were quickly picked up by looters, who fired them into the air and went on rampages.

headline: Judge Is Bulgaria's Premier
abstract: A politically independent judge who helped organize the country's first free elections was chosen Prime Minister today, a week after the resignation of a former Communist. Dimitar Popov, the head of Sofia's municipal court, was elected by a large majority of Parliament, the assembly's chairman announced. He said 15 deputies in the 400-member chamber had voted against Mr. Popov and 29 had abstained. headline: The Nation: A Campus Forum on Multiculturalism; Opening Academia Without Closing It Down
abstract: IS there such a thing as a disinterested Western cultural tradition, rooted in a commitment to rational inquiry and converging, century by century, on the truth? Or is "Western culture" in reality an ideology of white males who, in the name of progress and reason, have psychologically dominated the earth? In recent years, this debate has become especially heated on American campuses, with upholders of the Western tradition accusing their opponents of imposing their own ideology, based on calls for multiculturalism and a rejection of Western civilization. This supposed new orthodoxy is sometimes derisively called "the tyranny of the politically correct." The Week in Review asked people at several universities for their views from the front lines.  Educational Democracy    The tyranny of the politically correct? Multiculturalism as Exhibit A? You must be kidding. Perhaps unfortunate phrases, coined in California, play differently on the East Coast. Speaking from California, where the nonwhite population is rapidly becoming a statewide majority (and already is so in grades K through 12), dismissive talk about political correctness sounds just plain silly. The students are already in the classroom. They are diverse, and they do talk back.   If the pain of changes under way is great, the pain of no change is even greater. I remember what it was like as a Chicano in junior high school during the 1950's in Tucson, Ariz. The punishment was bending over, holding your ankles, and getting swats with a board. The crime was speaking Spanish on the playground. Somehow, fluency in Spanish was a deficit in elementary school and an achievement in college. When will we discover that diversity is a valuable resource?   Try beginning to teach a diverse classroom with: "We must first learn our heritage. It extends from Plato and Aristotle to Milton and Shakespeare." The students ask, "Who's the 'We' ?" At Stanford, over 40 percent of the entering undergraduates are Asian-Americans, African Americans, native Americans and Chicanos. Who, they wonder, is included in the phrase "our heritage?" Are they included? Must they continue to look into the curricular mirror and see nothing?   Sure, there's lip service, trendiness, insensitivity, confusion and all the rest. Sure, multiculturalism can sound inadequate or worse to those historically left out. But many people are also using multiculturalism as a tool for grappling with vexed issues. Newly diverse classrooms often do not work by the old rules. Newly selected texts cannot always be read in the old ways.   Educational democracy will not come easily. It will involve what I have come to call questions of cultural citizenship. How can diverse groups retain their diversity and participate in a democratic community? Can they be full and equal citizens who enjoy the privilege of shaping their destiny? Can they do so without having to surrender their heritages? -- Renato Rosaldo, Professor of Anthropology, Stanford University  'The Light of Reason Goes Out'     Deriding those who seek to understand the world, Marx said, "The point is to change it." That too is the point of "pluralist" academics who promote "diversity" and "multiculturalism." The terms are seriously misleading: one is naturally led to think of pluralists as fostering academically demanding programs requiring mastery of one or more foreign languages and thorough study of some (non-Western) culture(s). The agenda, however, is political: to transform an academy (ultimately, a society) that has "silenced" women and minorities. Pluralists tend to believe that the American university, supposedly liberal and humane, serves to perpetuate an oppressor class. (For feminists this is the "hetero-patriarchy"; more generally, it is the white, "Eurocentric" elite that "imposes prevailing cultural norms.") Finding the ideal of disinterested scholarship hypocritical, pluralists advocate a pedagogy that "empowers" students by alerting them to the need for struggle against partriarchy, racism and classism.   Pluralists tend to be latter-day Sophists, holding a Protagorean view that truth is not "out there" but "manmade." The contrasting phrases are Richard Rorty's, who has also said he finds no useful distinction between propaganda and the use of reason. Is it any wonder that pluralist classes tend to be "workshops" in consciousness-raising? When the intellectual is the political, the light of reason goes out. -- Frederic T. Sommers, Professor of Philosophy, Brandeis University  When Is Something 'Political'?    George Orwell once wrote that "no book is genuinely free from political bias. The opinion that art should have nothing to do with politics is itself a political attitude."    Orwell's point was that literature shapes our political attitudes all the more when it isn't explicitly    about    politics. Language silently thrusts all kinds of political assumptions on us if we don't become alert to them -- assumptions, for example, about whose sexuality is normal and abnormal and which groups have the right to run things.   Often, these assumptions are taken for granted as going without saying in the culture, as Milton took it for granted in "Paradise Lost" that Eve was mentally inferior to Adam, or as Tom Wolfe takes it for granted in "The Bonfire of the Vanities" that blacks will get out of hand if the whites who naturally run society don't have the guts to control them.   The Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe has said that no novel is ever politically neutral, because "even the attempt to say nothing about politics is a big political statement. You are saying, then, that everything is O.K." Yet I'm described as being political if I discuss a work's treatment of gender and race with my students, but if I don't mention such matters because I'm satisfied with the existing arrangements I'm not taken to be doing anything political. There's a double standard here: criticizing the status quo is political while accepting it isn't. -- Gerald Graff, Professor of English, Northwestern University Who's to Say What's 'Acceptable'     I am a black woman with a memory of what things were like before the advent of affirmative action, feminist theories, African-American studies, and diversified faculties and student bodies. I recall the time when virtually no people of color or white women taught at the great research universities, many of whose undergraduate student bodies were exclusively male.   In the 1960's and 1970's, most of academia rejected racial/ethnic and women's studies as narrowly particular, as though only nonwhite people had race and only nonmale people had gender. Hence black graduate students were warned away from racial topics, and women were told that if they wanted to be respected intellectually, they should avoid women's studies. We were steered toward more acceptable subjects, which were the lives and works of the wealthy, white and male.   In those days, the champions of orthodoxy described their own preoccupations in handsome, universal terms such as "truth" and "intrinsic worth." They disdained our ways of thinking as "political," while they wrapped themselves in the unassailable: "excellence."   I wish that those who take potshots at what they see as a new "political correctness" would give a thought to what American universities used to be like. Then, perhaps, they would hesitate before assailing the attempt to forge a pedagogy appropriate for newly diversified student bodies and faculties. -- Nell Irvin Painter, Professor of History, Princeton University  Indoctrination Is Not Education     The chief danger posed by academic leftists -- advocates of radical feminism, the normalization of homosexuality, Marxist revolution, and the like -- lies in the principled refusal of so many of them to allow others the space in which to articulate objections to their way of thinking -- space that is indispensable to survival of critical thought. When all dissent is immediately labeled as bigotry or ascribed to self-interest, dialogue and debate become impossible, and education degenerates into indoctrination. This poisonous process, most pronounced in literary and religious fields, has undone many of the most distinguished programs and faculties. Its antidote is something the radicals themselves often endorse loudly: diversity and pluralism. But they tend to define diversity exclusively by gender, race and sometimes class, ignoring the more subtle differences of intellectual and religious tradition and moral vision.   It is especially regrettable that the preoccupation with race tends to assimilate the experience of all whites to that of elite Protestant groups from northwestern Europe and helps perpetuate the anti-Catholicism still potent in academia. The source of this cramped definition of diversity is the neo-Marxist idea that class, race and gender determine consciousness. Ironic, is it not, that as so many nations discard the legacy of Marx, American professors embrace it all the more tightly?   The most alarming aspect of the current ideologization of academic life is the impression students receive that truth reduces to issues of power. As this impression spreads, the "deconstruction" of the university accelerates, for the transcendent horizon that alone justifies our enormous investment in humanistic education is not just ignored, but denied. -- Jon D. Levenson, Professor of Jewish Studies, Harvard Divinity School  'Europhobia' In the High Schools     We must urgently look at how these currently fashionable orthodoxies at the university level have begun to affect the public schools. Most pre-college students are too naive to understand how university-trained teachers or curriculum developers are manipulating them. And school committees and parents are usually totally unaware of what is going on because the Europhobia, national self-hatred and inter-ethnic hostilities that these orthodoxies are promoting have been cleverly disguised by current buzz words like multiculturalism, critical thinking and diversity.    All these terms can have straightforward and positive academic meanings, and in many school curriculum guides or individual courses they do. That is why manifestations of the ideology they cover up are difficult for unsophisticated parents to discern.   A current example of how a school committee is allowing a once outstanding academic curriculum to be transformed into a curriculum for political indoctrination is taking place right now in Brookline, Mass., where I live. Last year, the school committee voted to drop one of the high school's most popular and intellectually challenging courses -- Advanced Placement European History -- when its assistant superintendent for curriculum and most of the high school's social studies department argued that such a course was now incompatible with a multicultural curriculum. This year, large numbers of students have petitioned to have the course reinstated and obtained support from a legal ruling by the State Department of Education. High noon comes on Dec. 18, with a confused school committee caught between the intellectual demands of its own students and the fierce hostility of a Europhobic social studies department. If the course is reinstated, the department wants, as its pound of flesh, ninth graders henceforth to have to choose between taking European history in their sophomore year and taking the advanced placement course when they are seniors. If students are forced to forego as sophomores a European history course in order to be eligible for the advanced placement course as seniors, the remaining sophomore alternatives include a course in African-American history, which discusses the trans-Atlantic slave trade but conveniently omits discussion of the Arab slave trade in its coverage of African history, and another controversial course that focuses on three unrelated areas of conflict in the world: Northern Ireland, Vietnam and the Middle East. The school committee wants to believe that such courses are justified by the "needs" of the diverse population at the high school. The basic purpose of these and the other sophomore courses, however, is to balkanize students ethnically before they take U.S. history in grade 11 and to encourage them to view Britain, America and Israel as oppressor nations. -- Sandra Stotsky, Director, Summer Institute on Writing, Reading and Civic Education, Harvard Graduate School of Education  Weeding Outc The New Puritanism     Like the Puritans, the politically correct have an apparently desperate need to create an exclusive community. Their rituals are the conferences they attend; their liturgical language, an indecipherable jargon that belies their commitment to openness. Ultimately, American Puritanism centered itself around the need to distinguish between the saved and the damned. Making that distinction was an endless process, as it is for the politically correct. The saved -- in p.c. language, the "oppressed" -- are good no matter what they do; racial minorities, for instance, are, by definition, incapable of racism. The damned -- the white male "oppressors" of p.c. language -- are evil, even when they teach or act politically in favor of the oppressed.   But oppression is real, injustice based on gender, race and class is profound, pervasive and morally indefensible. The problem for the universities is not that the issues are less important than the politically correct make them, but that a Puritan style of reform is incompatible with the life of the mind. Many bonafide liberals have been startled to find themselves condemned, cursed, occasionally even physically attacked, by the politically correct. There is no room for the hesitations of reason in matters of faith.   There is a less noble dynamic at work here. Consider the endless possibilities political correctness holds out for research and publication, especially in the field of literature. Each new critical weapon opens the whole Western textual tradition to a new campaign of slash and burn. This is serious stuff. Academic careers are made and unmade in these waves of puritan heresy hunting. -- John E. Becker, Director of the Core Curriculum, Fairleigh Dickinson University, Madison, N.J. The Diversity Of Women's Studies     In fields such as women's studies, there is scarcely agreement on the assortment of positions claimed to be hegemonic. Currently there are over a half dozen ideological and theoretical "schools" in women's studies itself. Theories also overlap. Some conservative thinkers share with some radical feminists the belief that there are innate, biological differences between men and women. Arguments over the role of the state in the regulation of pornography and prostitution have allied conservatives with radical feminists against sexual liberals and libertarians. All of these disagreements form the basis for Women's (or Gender) Studies 101. While there is agreement that these issues should be discussed within the university by conservatives and radicals alike, there is not agreement among the scholars who adhere to and publish about these various schools of thought. -- Lois West, Assistant Professor of Sociology and Women's Studies, Florida International University  It's Not Simply 'Us vs. Them'     The criticism of political correctness usually comes in one of two versions: conservatives gripe about the politicization of academia (as if it had ever been unpolitical) and liberals whine about academic freedom (as if the issue were not precisely what that is). There are always only two sides to the issue, and if "we" are on the right side, "they" must be in the wrong.    I am interested in undercutting such binary logic. Rather than fruitlessly condemning the phenomenon, I would ask what makes p.c.-ness tick. I suspect that political correctness is much like other better-known fundamentalisms in that it is primarily concerned not with achieving its stated goals, but with preserving its own coherence. What counts about a fervent belief is not the belief itself (be it racial harmony, equality between the sexes, or the literal truth of the Bible) but the fervor with which it is held. People latch onto an orthodoxy because it provides them with a mental grid with which they organize their experience; the content of the orthodoxy is almost irrelevant.    A critique of political correctness need not imply a conservative political agenda; conservatives and p.c.-niks both like to give up contentious argument for orthodoxy, which puts a halt to thinking and takes the last bit of fun out of academia. -- Michel Chaouli, Department of Comparative Literature, University of California, Berkeley  A Bad Case of Academic Autism     'The 80's taught us a lesson about how the critical hairshirt could become more of a fashion statement than a political one.  In the old days, an academic book review might chastise a work of scholarship for inaccuracies in citation and such. Of late, for equally venial offenses, you'd probably be accused of complicity with the ideologies of oppression, of silencing all the wretched of the earth with a single paragraph. It is heady stuff: real politics never felt that good.   How did we come to appraise works of cultural criticism in terms more appropriate to combat? Academics made a pendular swing from the silly notion that scholarship existed wholly apart from politics to the equally silly position that everything we did had the very gravest political significance. We fell into what I call academic autism: close your eyes tight, recite the mantra of race-class-gender, and social problems will disappear.   A friend of mine cynically suggested that we institutionalize something that used to happen implicitly at conferences on "minority discourse" -- award a prize for the most oppressed speaker or respondent. At the end of the year, she added, we could hold a sort of Oppression Academy Awards ceremony. Once the invocation of oppression became another move in a game of academic one-upmanship, it was easy to lose sight of what's happening on the streets outside -- where almost half of the black children in this country live below the poverty line, and a black male in his 20's is more likely to end up in jail than in college.   Joining mood rings and Earth Shoes, "political correctness" has now entered into the realm of the merely facetious. Which isn't to say that the academy is no longer a theater for larger social conflicts. It's just that the academic intellectuals no longer have to pretend to know all the answers ahead of time. After all the shouting is over, is it too much to hope that the real conversation, long deferred, may begin? -- Henry Louis Gates Jr., Professor of English, Duke University

headline: STUDY DISCOURAGES CASH FOR SOVIETS
abstract: A report by four Western economic organizations to be made public Friday concludes that the Soviet Union faces more obstacles to economic health than most third-world countries and that its current disarray is such that a large amount of direct aid would be wasted.   Assessing the economy of the Soviet Union in much the same way they have the economies of Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, Nigeria and other troubled economies of the third world, the organizations' analysis is "very much in line" with the Administration's thinking, said a senior Bush Administration economic official, who asked not to be identified.

headline: Nigeria's Leader to Seek Slavery Reparations
abstract: The Nigerian President, Gen. Ibrahim Babangida, has called on Western nations to pay compensation to Africa for the damage done to the continent by the slave trade. headline: Africa Suffers From Leadership Problems
abstract: To the Editor:   You report that Nigeria's President, Ibrahim Babangida, speaking at a conference in Lagos, called on Western nations to pay compensation to Africa for damage done to the continent by the slave trade (news article, Dec. 24). While no one with a good sense of history will dispute that the slave trade wreaked incalculable havoc on the black race, it is preposterous to blame it for Africa's underdevelopment.   As a Nigerian living in the United States who travels frequently to Africa (I returned from Nigeria on Nov. 21), I have seen more damage done to that continent by incompetent and corrupt leadership than slavery ever did. The African landscape is awash with a class of leadership whose revolutionary songs were about ultimate redemption of the masses. Nevertheless, soon after they establish their rulership, they focus on personal enrichment. When things go wrong and the people start complaining, they resort to blame-the-West syndrome.   Was it the West that supervised the depletion of Nigeria's $100 billion oil fortune, earned between 1970 and 1980? Was it the West that was responsible for diverting much of those earnings to private bank accounts in Switzerland? Perhaps President Babangida should have explained to conference participants why Nigeria's telephone system hardly works?    Or is the West responsible for roads that are never maintained? Or is the West also responsible for the National Electric Power Authority's inability to deliver steady electric services to Nigerian homes?   How could any government that is worth its mettle spend so much time and effort persuading its citizens to learn to live with economic austerity measures only to turn around and sell its crude oil, its single most important source of revenue, at below-market price?   Instead of lavishing our energy on organizing conferences whose sole purpose is cheap self-serving international publicity, our attention should be on the serious problems confronting us. What better reparations can we give ourselves than making genuine efforts to improve our health-care system?    Our hospitals continue to operate at subsistence level; basic drugs are never available, and our doctors and nurses continue to flee to the West for better conditions of service.    Our educational system is far worse than in colonial days, all because of bad policy and neglect. Our judicial system is a joke because of persistent interference by successive rulers. Food is lacking because of bad agricultural policy. Basic transportation and shelter are hardly affordable because of inadequate planning.   Perhaps when we have helped ourselves, we can look to others for reparations.  C. CHUBA JON-NWAKALO  Albany, Dec. 25, 1990

headline: CHRONICLE
abstract: ZUBIN MEHTA , the music director of the New York Philharmonic, was to fly back to New York from Munich yesterday, but changed his mind and headed for Tel Aviv.    "He felt he needed to be in Israel" to demonstrate his affection for the country during the Persian Gulf crisis, said Neil Parker, a spokesman for the Philharmonic.    Mr. Mehta, who was born in Bombay, has also been the music director of the Israel Philharmonic since 1968. In 1981, the orchestra named him music director for life.    He had been in Austria to conduct the Vienna Philharmonic, then had driven to Munich for a flight to Paris, where he was to board the Concorde and return to New York. In Paris, he changed plans and flew to Israel instead.    "He feels that the entire country has adopted him and that it was not possible to be anywhere else at this moment but Israel," Mr. Parker said.   For the Philharmonic concerts on Thursday, Friday and next Tuesday, Mr. Mehta will be replaced by the assistant conductor, SAMUEL WONG . SHLOMO MINTZ , the solo violinist, will not be there, either. He has the flu and will be replaced by MARK PESKANOV .

headline: Review/Music; 3 Changes in One Concert
abstract: Repercussions from the war in the Persian Gulf were felt by the New York Philharmonic on Wednesday evening. Zubin Mehta was to have conducted the subscription concert, but in an insert in the program the orchestra's music director explained that in this time of crisis, "I know my place is in Israel." He left for Israel earlier in the week to show solidarity with its people and especially its musicians. Mr. Mehta, who is in his last season as music director of the New York Philharmonic, also holds the title of music director for life of the Israel Philharmonic.   Taking over the Avery Fisher Hall podium was Samuel Wong, a young assistant conductor. The change of conductors provided only one of the night's complications. Mr. Wong led a Haydn symphony, but not the one originally scheduled. There also was a replacement soloist: the violinist Mark Peskanov as soloist in Lalo's "Symphonie Espagnole," replacing Shlomo Mintz, who dropped out because of illness.

headline: New & Noteworthy
abstract: A TENURED PROFESSOR, by John Kenneth Galbraith. (Houghton Mifflin, $7.95.) After a Harvard economist discovers how to quantify the irrational side of economic behavior, he and his wife reap a fortune, devoting their sudden millions to making the world a nicer place. Last year our reviewer, Barbara Ehrenreich, called the novel "a liberal wish-fulfillment fantasy, transmuting greed to good with rollicking zeal. Along the way, Mr. Galbraith has great fun at the expense of the powerful and their all-too-numerous admirers."   JAZZ CLEOPATRA: Josephine Baker in Her Time, by Phyllis Rose. (Vintage, $12.95.) The daughter of a St. Louis laundrywoman, the dancer Josephine Baker caused a sensation in the clubs of Paris when she appeared onstage wearing little more than a skirt of bananas. Later she became known for her work as a spy in the French Resistance, as a campaigner for civil rights in the United States and as the matriarch of a multiracial family of adopted children she called the Rainbow Tribe. In 1989 The Times's Michiko Kakutani said Phyllis Rose "has a gift for combining biography with literary, social and psychological analysis, and there are passages in 'Jazz Cleopatra' where this talent shines."   FOR THE SAKE OF ALL LIVING THINGS, by John M. Del Vecchio. (Bantam, $5.95.) While her brother is working as a leader of the Khmer Rouge, a Cambodian woman falls in love with an American adviser to the Government in Phnom Penh. Last year our reviewer, David Murray, said the novel succeeds because of "the power of Mr. Del Vecchio's prose and the enormous amount of information he submits to his readers. He has added another memorable book to the literature of the Southeast Asian conflict, a tragic, bloody saga that seems to be with us forever."   ISARA: A Voyage Around "Essay," by Wole Soyinka. (Vintage International, $9.95.) In a book that is part imagination, part fact, Wole Soyinka, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986, tells about his father, a teacher named Essay, and his life in colonial Nigeria. The book "goes far beyond a homage," Rita Dove said here in 1989. "It supplies the essential ingredient missing from history books -- not only the Zeitgeist, but the heart that propels the spirit."   ADVANCE, RETREAT: Selected Short Stories, by Richard Rive. (St. Martin's, $10.95.) Written by a South African who was found murdered in his home in 1989, these short stories tell what it is like to be of mixed race in the land of apartheid. "Richard Rive's historical place in the development of South African literature is assured," Tony Eprile said here last year. "This humane, sharply observant collection of stories shows that his is a voice to be discovered by each new reader, a voice that lingers long after one has read the stories."   THE COMING GLOBAL BOOM: How to Benefit Now From Tomorrow's Dynamic World Economy, by Charles R. Morris. (Bantam, $12.95.) Despite the prevailing view of the doomsayers, an economist argues, the world is on the verge of an unprecedented boom. "Charles R. Morris is not afraid of optimism," Adam Smith said here last year. "In 'The Coming Global Boom' he has once again set himself up as contrarian critic, and has published a bullish argument in lively form."   TIME'S WITNESS, by Michael Malone. (Pocket Books, $5.95.) The police chief of a small town in North Carolina uncovers a web of corruption when he investigates the murder of a local black political leader. In 1989 our reviewer, Valerie Sayers, said the novel offers "a complex and satisfying plot, a rich panorama of a class-stratified Southern town and dense portraits of even minor characters."   DOWN THE RIVER, by Edward Abbey. (Plume, $9.95.) When these essays by Edward Abbey, the patron saint of environmental guerrillas and nature-loving misanthropes, were published in 1982, our reviewer, Tim Cahill, said, "He can write movingly about the most simple outdoor pleasures: planting a tree, seeing a bear, watching hawks in flight, getting drunk." THE JOURNEY HOME: Some Words in Defense of the American West (Plume, $9.95) shows Abbey as an "American artifact, part maverick, part pastoral extremist, part semi-hermit, part latter-day Jeremiah Johnson," Ted Morgan said here in 1977. The publisher has also reissued two other books by the author, who died in 1989: ABBEY'S ROAD ($9.95), a 1979 collection of wilderness essays, and GOOD NEWS ($10.95), a 1980 novel set in a future time when American civilization has fallen apart, replaced by a preindustrial economy of whites and Indians living off the bounty of the West.    ANY WOMAN'S BLUES, by Erica Jong. (Harper Paperbacks, $5.95.) As she approaches middle age, the liberated heroine of "Fear of Flying" finds herself grounded by an addiction to sex, drugs and an abusive young boyfriend named Darton Venable Donegal 4th. Last year our reviewer, Benjamin DeMott, said he liked "Fear of Flying" better but that "an occasional idiom or patch of comic invention elsewhere calls up Ms. Jong's earlier achievements."   EAST OF CHOSIN: Entrapment and Breakout in Korea, 1950, by Roy E. Appleman. (Texas A&M University, $14.95.) Through interviews with survivors and other sources, a historian of the Korean War tells what happened when American forces at Chosin Reservoir were surprised by a regiment of the Chinese Army. "For most Americans, knowledge of the Korean War is both scant and vague," Bernard E. Trainor said here in 1987. This book "deals at once sympathetically and analytically with one of the painful episodes of that struggle."

headline: Robert F. Bonner, 55, Environment Engineer
abstract: Robert F. Bonner Jr., a professional engineer and an officer with Malcolm Pirnie, Inc., one of the nation's largest environmental engineering companies, died Sunday at his home in Hampton, Va. He was 55 years old.   He died of cancer, a funeral home representative said.   Mr. Bonner, who directed the design and construction of some of the nation's largest water treatment plants, began his career with Malcolm Pirnie in 1965. He was named a vice president in 1973 and a corporate director in 1979. He became senior corporate officer for the company's regional headquarters in Newport News, Va., in 1984.    Mr. Bonner, a graduate of Villanova University and the Newark College of Engineering, had previously worked on environmental projects in Iran and Nigeria with the firm of Sidney Bowne of Manhattan.    He is survived by his wife, the former Linda Hanifin, head of a public relations firm; a daughter, Christina Bonner of Orlando, Fla.; a son, Tyrus of White Plains; a sister, Anne Bonner of Manhattan; two brothers, Frederick of Baltimore and Edward of Westbury, L.I.; and a grandson.

headline: Never Saw a Protest I Didn't Like, but Now. . .
abstract: To the Editor:   Having grown up in the 1960's, I've never seen a protest I didn't like. I might not have always agreed with the shouted objectives or postered profanities, but it seemed such an American thing to do. Our house in Amsterdam, N.Y., always flew the Stars and Stripes on national holidays at a time few others did. The only thing that disturbed me more than seeing protesters burn the American flag was finding out how few of my fellow citizens bothered to vote.   In times past I fasted for Biafra (remember?), marched on Washington for peace in Vietnam and was arrested for blocking the draft board in Albany. Still wanting to do my patriotic bit, I served in the Peace Corps. I've lobbied against U.S. involvement in Central America. In 1989 I even got my face in Newsweek for demonstrating on behalf of free speech in the Salman Rushdie affair.   Of late I have petitioned the President and written letters to my Congressional representative not to go to war in the Persian Gulf. Now that we are at war, things have changed.   I will not be participating in this Saturday's march on Washington. Oh, I had planned to join the demonstrators in Times Square the day after fighting started but I didn't go. My heart wasn't in it.   I've tried to understand my lack of enthusiasm. One difference is that this time the President asked Congress for permission to commit our troops to battle. This doesn't make the war right or moral, but it does reinforce our heretofore badly abused Constitution. More important, unlike Vietnam, where the body bags started coming home years before U.S. citizens realized a war was going on, this time we've all had months to make our views known.   If nothing else, we shall soon learn whether the "lesson of Vietnam" is that the United States should muzzle the media while hitting the enemy with everything we've got (as the Pentagon seems to believe), or instead that technological and military superiority don't always defeat a people determined to defend their home soil or sand, as the case may be.   And so I pray and cry and tie yellow ribbons on my door. Once this nightmare is over, I sincerely hope all Americans will ask our elected officials just how and why we got ourselves into this mess -- and then shout, march and vote accordingly. (Rev.) JOSEPH R. VENEROSO Maryknoll, N.Y., Jan. 24, 1991
